q: What were the first "books" of ancient Mesopotamia made of?
fact: The Sumerians wrote in cuneiform on wet clay tablets, which were then dried in the sun or fired.

q: From which plant did the ancient Egyptians make their main writing material?
fact: Papyrus stalks were cut into strips, laid crosswise and pressed together to make sheets for scrolls.

q: Who became the first emperor of ancient Rome?
fact: Caesar was a dictator, not an emperor. Octavian received the title "Augustus" in 27 BC.

q: Which bird appeared on the famous silver coins of ancient Athens?
fact: The owl was the symbol of Athena, the city's patron goddess. Athenian tetradrachms were simply called "owls".

q: Which country sponsored Columbus's voyage of 1492?
fact: Columbus was born in Genoa, but the expedition was funded by the Spanish monarchs Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon.

q: Who introduced printing with movable type to Europe?
fact: Gutenberg began printing in Mainz around 1450. His most famous work is the 42-line Bible.

q: Who set up the first printing press in England, in 1476?
fact: Caxton set up his press at Westminster. One of the first books he printed there was Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales.

q: Which brothers created the first Slavic alphabet in the 9th century?
fact: Around 863 Constantine (later the monk Cyril) created the Glagolitic script. The Cyrillic alphabet was later named after him.

q: Which English king broke with Rome and made himself head of the Church of England?
fact: The Act of Supremacy of 1534 followed the Pope's refusal to annul Henry's marriage to Catherine of Aragon.

q: In which year did Peter the Great found St. Petersburg?
fact: In May 1703 the Peter and Paul Fortress was laid down on Hare Island, and the city's history is counted from then.

q: In which year did Russia abolish serfdom?
fact: Tsar Alexander II's manifesto of 1861 freed about 23 million serfs owned by landlords.

q: Which is the oldest university in the English-speaking world?
fact: Teaching at Oxford existed by 1096. Cambridge was founded in 1209 by scholars who left Oxford.

q: In which year did Britain and its colonies switch to the Gregorian calendar?
fact: In September 1752, Wednesday the 2nd was followed by Thursday the 14th: eleven days were simply skipped.

q: What did Peter the Great tax to push Russian men toward European fashion?
fact: A man who paid the beard tax received a copper token reading "Money taken", which he had to carry with him.

q: What was the silver coin that formed the basis of ancient Rome's currency for centuries?
fact: The denarius was first minted around 211 BC. The "d" in Britain's old pounds, shillings and pence stood for denarius.

q: Before decimalization in 1971, how many pennies were in a British shilling?
fact: There were 12 pence in a shilling and 20 shillings in a pound, so a pound was worth 240 pence.

q: What fraction of a penny was the old British farthing?
fact: The name comes from Old English feorthing, "a fourth part". The farthing stopped being legal tender in 1961.

q: Who was the tutor of the young Alexander the Great?
fact: King Philip II invited Aristotle to teach his son. Lessons went on for several years at Mieza, near Pella.

q: On which river did ancient Babylon stand?
fact: Babylon lay on the Euphrates in modern Iraq, about 85 km south of Baghdad.

q: Which Babylonian king is known for a law code carved on a stone stele?
fact: The stele with Hammurabi's laws (18th century BC) was found at Susa and is now kept in the Louvre.

q: Which people created the alphabet that became the ancestor of Greek writing?
fact: The Greeks borrowed the Phoenician alphabet and added letters for vowel sounds.

q: Which find helped Champollion decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs?
fact: The stone carries the same decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic script and Greek. Champollion announced his decipherment in 1822.

q: Where were the Olympic Games held in ancient Greece?
fact: Olympia was a sanctuary of Zeus in the Peloponnese. The traditional date of the first Games is 776 BC.

q: Who is the Julian calendar named after?
fact: The calendar was introduced by decree of Julius Caesar and took effect in 45 BC.

q: Which pope introduced the Gregorian calendar in 1582?
fact: To correct an accumulated error, October 4, 1582 was followed directly by October 15.

q: What was the name of Columbus's flagship on his 1492 voyage?
fact: The Santa Maria sailed with the caravels Pinta and Nina. The flagship ran aground off the island of Hispaniola.

q: Whose expedition made the first voyage around the world in 1519-1522?
fact: Magellan himself was killed in the Philippines. Juan Sebastian Elcano completed the voyage aboard the Victoria.

q: Who was the first European to sail to India around Africa?
fact: Da Gama reached India in 1498. Dias had rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488 but never got to India.

q: Which navigator gave his name to the Americas?
fact: Mapmaker Martin Waldseemuller suggested the name on a 1507 map, since Vespucci had written that a New World was found.

q: Who led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in 1911?
fact: Amundsen's team reached the Pole on December 14, 1911, about five weeks before Scott's party.

q: Which Englishman was the first captain to sail his own ship around the world, in 1577-1580?
fact: Drake sailed the Golden Hind and was knighted by Elizabeth I aboard it in 1581.

q: Which strait between Asia and America is named after a Dane in Russian service?
fact: It is named after Vitus Bering, although the Cossack Semyon Dezhnev sailed through it first, in 1648.

q: Which inventor is the unit of power, the watt, named after?
fact: Watt improved the steam engine by adding a separate condenser, making it far more efficient.

q: Who built the first working railway steam locomotive, in 1804?
fact: Trevithick's engine hauled 10 tons of iron along a tramway at Penydarren in Wales.

q: Which was the first public railway to run steam trains, opening in 1825?
fact: It opened on September 27, 1825, with George Stephenson's Locomotion No. 1 pulling the first train.

q: Who created the first electric battery, the "voltaic pile"?
fact: Around 1800 Volta stacked alternating zinc and copper discs separated by pads soaked in brine.

q: Which 18th-century scientist invented the lightning rod?
fact: Franklin studied atmospheric electricity in the 1750s and showed that lightning is an electrical discharge.

q: Which English king sealed the Magna Carta in 1215?
fact: The barons forced King John to limit his own power. The charter is seen as a cornerstone of English law.

q: Which Chinese emperor was buried with the Terracotta Army?
fact: The army of thousands of clay soldiers was found by chance in 1974 by farmers digging a well near Xi'an.

q: Where did the decimal numerals that Europeans call "Arabic" originate?
fact: Arabs adopted the Indian numerals, zero included, and passed them on to Europe, hence the name.

q: The word "parchment" comes from the name of which ancient city?
fact: Pergamon in Asia Minor was famous for producing a writing material from finely prepared animal skin.

q: Where was the Sutton Hoo ship burial discovered in 1939?
fact: The Anglo-Saxon grave, probably of King Raedwald of East Anglia, held a famous helmet and gold treasures.

q: Which Byzantine emperor ordered the great codification of Roman law in the 6th century?
fact: The Corpus Juris Civilis (529-534) became the foundation of civil law across much of Europe.

q: What did the Romans call the town they founded on the Thames around AD 47-50?
fact: Londinium was burned by Queen Boudica's rebels around AD 60-61 but was soon rebuilt.

q: Which English king was known as "the Confessor"?
fact: Edward the Confessor built Westminster Abbey, consecrated in 1065 just before his death. He was made a saint in 1161.

q: Which Chinese dynasty built most of the Great Wall that survives today?
fact: Most of the brick and stone wall that tourists see today dates from the Ming dynasty (1368-1644).

q: Which Kremlin relic, weighing about 200 tons, has never rung because it cracked in a fire?
fact: It was cast by Ivan and Mikhail Motorin. In the 1737 fire it was still in its casting pit and cracked when doused with water.

q: Which English king hid in an oak tree after losing the Battle of Worcester in 1651?
fact: The "Royal Oak" at Boscobel became a legend, and many British pubs are still named after it.

q: Which is the oldest British order of chivalry, founded by Edward III around 1348?
fact: Its motto is "Honi soit qui mal y pense". Membership is limited to the monarch, the Prince of Wales and 24 companions.

q: How many articles did the original US Constitution of 1787 contain?
fact: The Constitution has seven articles. The first ten amendments form the Bill of Rights; there are 27 amendments in all.

q: Which newspaper did Benjamin Franklin take over in 1729?
fact: Franklin made the Gazette one of the most successful papers in the colonies. He also published Poor Richard's Almanack.

q: Catherine the Great of Russia was born a princess of which nationality?
fact: Born Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst in 1729, she converted to Orthodoxy and took the name Yekaterina Alekseyevna.

q: Which empress is considered the founder of the Hermitage Museum?
fact: The museum dates its founding to 1764, when Catherine bought a collection of paintings from the Berlin merchant Gotzkowsky.

q: Which country issued Europe's first banknotes, in 1661?
fact: They were issued by Stockholms Banco. Sweden's copper plate money was so heavy that paper notes were a relief.

q: What did the Pony Express carry across the American West in 1860-1861?
fact: Riders relayed mail about 1,900 miles from Missouri to California in about 10 days. The telegraph soon made it obsolete.

q: Which Roman emperor ordered a wall built across Britain in AD 122?
fact: Hadrian's Wall ran about 117 km from coast to coast and marked the northern frontier of the Roman province.

q: Which English state institution did Isaac Newton run for many years?
fact: Newton served at the Royal Mint from 1696 until his death, oversaw a recoinage and hunted down counterfeiters.

q: Who received a patent in 1886 for a gasoline-powered car, considered the world's first?
fact: Benz's Motorwagen had three wheels. In 1888 his wife Bertha drove it more than 100 km.

q: Which brothers held the first paid public film screening in Paris in 1895?
fact: The screening took place on December 28, 1895, at the Grand Cafe on the Boulevard des Capucines.

q: What was the early photographic process presented in France in 1839 called?
fact: It was named after Louis Daguerre. The image was formed on a silver-plated copper sheet.

q: What were the multi-story apartment blocks of ancient Rome called?
fact: The urban poor lived in insulae. Ground floors often held shops, and the top-floor flats were the cheapest.

q: Which city was the main center of the medieval Hanseatic League?
fact: Lubeck was called the "Queen of the Hanse". The league of northern trading towns even had an office in Novgorod.

q: What is the name of Iceland's ancient parliament, founded in 930?
fact: The Althing first met in the open air at Thingvellir and is often called one of the oldest parliaments in the world.

q: Who wrote "The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire"?
fact: It came out in six volumes from 1776 to 1789. The first volume appeared the same year as the US Declaration of Independence.

q: Which famous English school was founded by King Henry VI in 1440?
fact: Eton has educated 20 British prime ministers, along with many other public figures.

q: Who had the exotic Royal Pavilion built in Brighton?
fact: It was built for George as Prince of Wales and Prince Regent. John Nash gave it its Indian-style exterior.

q: Which museum, opened in Oxford in 1683, is often called Britain's first public museum?
fact: It was built to house the collection of curiosities that Elias Ashmole gave to the University of Oxford.

q: What was Henry Tate, founder of London's Tate gallery, by trade?
fact: Tate made his fortune refining sugar, including sugar cubes. His gallery opened at Millbank in 1897.

q: Which daughter of Yaroslav the Wise of Kyiv became Queen of France?
fact: Anne of Kyiv married King Henry I of France and was the mother of King Philip I.

q: Whose nearly intact tomb was found in the Valley of the Kings in 1922?
fact: The tomb was opened by Howard Carter. Inside were thousands of objects and the famous golden funerary mask.

q: What was the origin of the dynasty to which Cleopatra VII belonged?
fact: The Ptolemies descended from one of Alexander the Great's generals. According to Plutarch, Cleopatra was the first of them to learn Egyptian.

q: The word "laconic" comes from which region of Greece?
fact: Laconia was the region around Sparta, and Spartans were famous for speaking briefly and to the point.

q: In the earliest Roman calendar, which month of the year was September?
fact: The year began in March, so September comes from Latin septem, "seven". Likewise, October was the eighth.

q: What did the chronicles of medieval Rus call Scandinavian Vikings?
fact: The famous trade route "from the Varangians to the Greeks" ran along the Dnieper from the Baltic to Byzantium.

q: Which Viking reached North America around the year 1000?
fact: Leif called the land Vinland. A Viking settlement has been found at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland.

q: Which French king made Versailles his main residence?
fact: The "Sun King" turned his father's hunting lodge into a palace and moved the court there in 1682.

q: On which island did Napoleon Bonaparte spend his final days?
fact: Napoleon died on Saint Helena in the Atlantic in 1821. He was born on Corsica and first exiled to Elba.

q: What was George Stephenson's locomotive that won the 1829 trials called?
fact: At the Rainhill Trials only Rocket passed every test. It was chosen for the Liverpool and Manchester Railway.

q: In which city did the world's first underground railway open in 1863?
fact: The first underground trains were pulled by steam engines, and the tunnels were ventilated through special openings.

q: What was the world's first postage stamp, issued in 1840, called?
fact: The British stamp showed young Queen Victoria's profile and paid for a letter weighing up to half an ounce.

q: Which number system did the Sumerians use, leaving us 60 minutes in an hour?
fact: Mesopotamia's legacy includes 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle.

q: Which Chinese official is traditionally credited with inventing paper around AD 105?
fact: Cai Lun reported to the emperor on paper made from bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets.

q: What was the Inca system of recording with knotted cords called?
fact: Quipus were strings with knots. Their type, color and position kept track of taxes, people and supplies.

q: Which metal tablet gave Mongol officials and envoys safe passage across the empire?
fact: The Polos received golden paizas from Kublai Khan, which protected them on their long journey home.

q: Which city was the traveler Marco Polo from?
fact: The Venetian dictated the book of his travels while held prisoner in Genoa to the writer Rustichello of Pisa.

q: Which Moroccan traveler spent nearly 30 years crossing the 14th-century world?
fact: Ibn Battuta set out from Tangier in 1325 and traveled some 117,000 km, from West Africa to China.

q: In old English homes, what was a rushlight?
fact: The pith of a rush was soaked in kitchen fat and burned in the evening as a cheap substitute for costly candles.

q: Which architect designed the great dome of Florence Cathedral?
fact: Completed in 1436, Brunelleschi's dome is still the largest brick dome ever built.

q: Roughly how much is one British "stone"?
fact: A stone is 14 pounds, or 6.35 kg. Britons still often give their body weight in stones.

q: What was the room in a medieval monastery where books were copied called?
fact: Before printing, monk scribes spent months copying a single book by hand on parchment.

q: Which ship carried the Pilgrims to America in 1620?
fact: About 102 passengers sailed from Plymouth, England, and founded Plymouth Colony in what is now Massachusetts.

q: Who became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, in 1932?
fact: Earhart flew from Newfoundland to Northern Ireland in about 15 hours, five years to the day after Lindbergh's flight.

q: Which medieval monk gave the musical notes their names (ut, re, mi...)?
fact: Guido took the first syllables of the lines of a Latin hymn. The syllable ut was later replaced by do.

q: Who was the last Byzantine emperor, killed when Constantinople fell in 1453?
fact: Constantine XI Palaiologos died defending the walls as Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II took the city.

q: Which royal house ruled England from 1485 to 1603?
fact: The dynasty began with Henry VII after the Battle of Bosworth and ended with the death of Elizabeth I.

q: What did the Romans use to build the dome of the Pantheon, standing for nearly 2,000 years?
fact: Roman concrete was made with volcanic ash. The Pantheon's dome has no steel reinforcement and has stood since the 2nd century.

q: Which king ordered the creation of the Korean Hangul alphabet in 1443?
fact: Hangul made reading easier for commoners who struggled with Chinese characters. Korea celebrates Hangul Day on October 9.

q: Which gold coin did Florence begin minting in 1252?
fact: The florin was named after the city and became a standard coin across Europe for centuries. The Venetian ducat appeared in 1284.

q: What was the capital of the Golden Horde?
fact: Sarai stood on the lower Volga. Karakorum was the capital of the whole Mongol Empire.

q: Where was the game that became the ancestor of chess invented?
fact: The ancient Indian game chaturanga represented four army divisions: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots.

q: Which lake is the deepest on Earth?
fact: Lake Baikal reaches a depth of about 1,642 meters, and its age is estimated at 25 million years.

q: What is the capital of Australia?
fact: Canberra was purpose-built as a compromise when Sydney and Melbourne both claimed the title of capital.

q: Which river is the longest in Europe?
fact: The Volga is about 3,530 km long. It flows into the Caspian Sea, which has no link to the world ocean.

q: In which country is Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest peak?
fact: Kilimanjaro, about 5,895 m high, stands in Tanzania near the equator, yet its summit has glaciers.

q: Which strait separates Eurasia from North America?
fact: At its narrowest the Bering Strait is about 86 km wide, with the Diomede Islands in the middle.

q: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
fact: The Sahara covers about 9 million square kilometers, and the word sahra simply means "desert" in Arabic.

q: What is the highest peak in the contiguous United States?
fact: Mount Whitney in California rises 4,421 m, only about 135 km from Death Valley, the lowest point in North America.

q: What is the capital of Canada?
fact: Queen Victoria chose Ottawa in 1857 as a compromise between English-speaking Toronto and French-speaking Montreal.

q: Counting all its territories, which country has the most time zones?
fact: Thanks to overseas territories from Polynesia to Reunion, France has 12 time zones, while Russia has 11.

q: Which sea has no coastline?
fact: The Sargasso Sea in the Atlantic is bounded not by land but by ocean currents. It is famous for its floating seaweed.

q: The shore of which body of water is the lowest point on dry land?
fact: The surface of the Dead Sea lies about 430 m below sea level and is still dropping.

q: Where is Angel Falls, the world's tallest waterfall?
fact: Angel Falls is about 979 m high. It is named after the American pilot Jimmie Angel.

q: Which river flows through the most countries?
fact: The Danube flows through 10 countries and past four capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.

q: Which river carries the most water in the world?
fact: The Amazon accounts for about a fifth of all the river water that reaches the world's oceans.

q: Which national capital lies farthest south?
fact: New Zealand's capital, Wellington, lies at about 41 degrees south and is famous for its strong winds.

q: Which of these rivers flows into the Arctic Ocean?
fact: The Mackenzie, Canada's longest river, empties into the Beaufort Sea of the Arctic Ocean.

q: Off the coast of which country live the only penguins found at the equator?
fact: The Galapagos penguin lives on Ecuador's Galapagos Islands, where cold ocean currents keep it cool.

q: What does a koala eat in the wild?
fact: Eucalyptus leaves are low in nutrients and toxic to many animals, so koalas save energy by sleeping up to 20 hours a day.

q: Which tree did the US Congress name America's national tree in 2004?
fact: The oak was chosen after a public vote organized by the Arbor Day Foundation, beating the redwood.

q: Which tree is known as the "monkey bread tree"?
fact: Monkeys love baobab fruit, and the tree's thick trunk can store thousands of liters of water for droughts.

q: Which tree is the tallest in the world?
fact: A California coast redwood named Hyperion is about 115 m tall, higher than a 35-story building.

q: What causes the northern lights?
fact: Charged particles from the Sun hit Earth's magnetic field and make gases in the upper atmosphere glow.

q: In which US national park is the Old Faithful geyser?
fact: Yellowstone, founded in 1872 as the world's first national park, holds about half of all the geysers on Earth.

q: Where was the highest air temperature on Earth, 56.7 C, officially recorded?
fact: It was recorded in July 1913 at Furnace Creek. An older Libyan reading of 58 C was rejected by the WMO in 2012.

q: Which river flows through Washington, D.C.?
fact: The Potomac forms much of the border between Maryland and Virginia. George Washington's Mount Vernon overlooks it.

q: Which waterway does New York's Brooklyn Bridge cross?
fact: The East River is actually a tidal strait. The Brooklyn Bridge opened across it in 1883.

q: At the meeting of which two rivers does Pittsburgh stand?
fact: The two rivers join at a spot called the Point to form the Ohio River. Pittsburgh is nicknamed the City of Bridges.

q: Which river does Prague's Charles Bridge cross?
fact: The Vltava is the longest river in the Czech Republic. Construction of the Charles Bridge began in 1357.

q: What is the capital of Morocco, even though Casablanca is bigger?
fact: Rabat lies on the Atlantic coast at the mouth of the Bou Regreg River and became the capital under the French protectorate in 1912.

q: Which city is the de facto capital of Switzerland?
fact: The Swiss constitution names no capital: Bern is officially the "federal city".

q: Which city replaced Lagos as Nigeria's capital in 1991?
fact: Abuja was built almost from scratch to a master plan in the middle of the country, far from crowded coastal Lagos.

q: Which country is completely surrounded by South Africa?
fact: All of Lesotho lies more than 1,000 m above sea level, which is true of no other country.

q: Which country stretches over 4,000 km from north to south but averages only about 180 km wide?
fact: Chile runs along the Andes from the Atacama Desert in the north to the glaciers of Tierra del Fuego in the south.

q: Which of these South American countries is landlocked?
fact: South America has only two landlocked countries: Bolivia and Paraguay.

q: Which lake is the largest in Europe?
fact: Lake Ladoga, near St. Petersburg, covers about 17,900 square kilometers. The Neva River flows out of it.

q: Lake Titicaca lies on the border of which two countries?
fact: Titicaca lies at about 3,800 m and is considered the highest navigable lake in the world.

q: What is Mount Everest called in Nepal?
fact: In Tibet the mountain is called Chomolungma, while in Nepal it is Sagarmatha, "forehead of the sky".

q: Which is the longest mountain range on land?
fact: The Andes run more than 7,000 km along the western edge of South America through seven countries.

q: Which mountains are traditionally considered the border between Europe and Asia?
fact: The conventional boundary between the two continents runs along the Urals, marked by monuments along the way.

q: In which ocean is the Mariana Trench, the deepest place on Earth?
fact: The Mariana Trench is nearly 11 km deep: Mount Everest would fit inside it with room to spare.

q: Which sea is considered the saltiest sea connected to the world ocean?
fact: The Red Sea's salinity reaches about 41 parts per thousand: no rivers flow into it and evaporation is intense.

q: Which warm current makes Western Europe's climate milder?
fact: The Gulf Stream and its extension, the North Atlantic Current, carry tropical heat toward Europe's shores.

q: Which Arctic port stays ice-free in winter thanks to a warm current?
fact: Murmansk lies on the Kola Bay, which warm Atlantic waters reach, so the port works all year round.

q: What are tropical cyclones called in the northwestern Pacific?
fact: It is the same phenomenon: near the Americas it is called a hurricane, near Asia a typhoon.

q: Which of these countries does the equator pass through?
fact: The equator crosses Kenya almost through the middle and also passes through Uganda, Somalia, Congo and Gabon.

q: Where does most of the International Date Line run?
fact: The line roughly follows the 180th meridian: crossing it westward, the calendar jumps a day ahead.

q: Which Italian city is built on more than a hundred islands in a lagoon?
fact: Venice sits on about 118 small islands linked by hundreds of bridges over its canals.

q: Which of these capitals lies at the highest elevation?
fact: Ecuador's capital, Quito, lies at about 2,850 m, very close to the equator.

q: Niagara Falls lies on the border of which two countries?
fact: The Niagara River flows from Lake Erie to Lake Ontario, and the falls consist of three parts.

q: On which river are Victoria Falls?
fact: Locals call the falls Mosi-oa-Tunya, "the smoke that thunders"; the spray can be seen from miles away.

q: Iguazu Falls lie on the border of which two countries?
fact: Iguazu is a system of about 275 waterfalls stretching for nearly 3 km.

q: Where do lemurs live in the wild?
fact: All lemur species are native only to Madagascar and the nearby Comoros Islands and live nowhere else in the wild.

q: In which country does the Komodo dragon, the world's largest lizard, live?
fact: The Komodo dragon lives on several Indonesian islands and can grow up to 3 m long.

q: Which flightless bird is a symbol of New Zealand?
fact: A kiwi's nostrils are at the tip of its beak, so it hunts by smell. New Zealanders are jokingly called "Kiwis" too.

q: Which bird can fly backwards?
fact: A hummingbird beats its wings dozens of times per second and can hover in place like a helicopter.

q: What is stored in a camel's hump?
fact: Hump fat is an energy reserve. Keeping it in one place rather than all over the body helps the camel stay cool.

q: What color is a polar bear's skin?
fact: Dark skin absorbs the sun's heat well, while the bear's fur is actually colorless and hollow.

q: Why are flamingo feathers pink?
fact: Flamingos eat shrimp and algae rich in carotenoids. Without such food their feathers slowly fade.

q: Roughly how far can an owl turn its head?
fact: An owl's eyes cannot move in their sockets, so it has to turn its head instead.

q: Which plant family does bamboo belong to?
fact: Bamboo is a giant grass, a relative of wheat. Some species can grow almost a meter in a day.

q: Where does the potato come from originally?
fact: Native peoples of the Andes domesticated the potato thousands of years ago; the Spanish brought it to Europe in the 16th century.

q: Which plant has the largest single flower in the world?
fact: A Rafflesia flower can be up to a meter across and smells of rotting meat to attract flies.

q: Which plant catches insects by snapping its trap-like leaves shut?
fact: The flytrap's trap closes when its sensitive hairs are touched twice in quick succession.

q: Which volcano's eruption destroyed Pompeii in AD 79?
fact: Ash from Vesuvius buried Pompeii and preserved the city almost intact. It has been excavated since the 18th century.

q: Which is the highest active volcano in Eurasia?
fact: Klyuchevskaya Sopka on Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula rises almost 4.8 km and erupts regularly.

q: The word "geyser" comes from the name of a hot spring in which country?
fact: The word comes from Iceland's Geysir, whose name is related to a word meaning "to gush".

q: Along the edges of which ocean does the volcanic "Ring of Fire" run?
fact: Most of the planet's active volcanoes lie along the Pacific Ring of Fire.

q: Which color is on the outer edge of a rainbow?
fact: In a primary rainbow red is always on the outside, while a fainter secondary rainbow has the colors reversed.

q: Which US state is the largest by area?
fact: Alaska is more than twice the size of Texas. The United States bought it from Russia in 1867.

q: Which is the largest country in Africa by area?
fact: Algeria became Africa's largest country in 2011, when South Sudan split off from Sudan.

q: Which is the northernmost capital of a sovereign state?
fact: Reykjavik lies at about 64 degrees north and is heated mainly by hot water from underground springs.

q: Which is the largest peninsula in the world?
fact: The Arabian Peninsula covers about 3 million square kilometers, most of it taken up by Saudi Arabia.

q: Which oceans does the Panama Canal connect?
fact: The Panama Canal opened in 1914; ships are raised above sea level by a system of locks.

q: Which seas does the Suez Canal connect?
fact: The Suez Canal opened in 1869. It lets ships sail from Europe to Asia without going around Africa.

q: Which strait separates Europe from Africa?
fact: At its narrowest the Strait of Gibraltar is about 14 km wide: on a clear day Africa is visible from Spain.

q: Which strait separates Great Britain from France?
fact: The Channel Tunnel, about 50 km long, runs beneath the English Channel. It opened in 1994.

q: Which cape is the southernmost point of Africa?
fact: Many people think it is the Cape of Good Hope, but that lies farther west and slightly north of Cape Agulhas.

q: Which cape is the northernmost point of mainland Eurasia?
fact: Cape Chelyuskin on Russia's Taymyr Peninsula is named after navigator Semyon Chelyuskin, who reached it in 1742.

q: What is the largest island of the United States?
fact: The Big Island covers about 10,400 square kilometers, more than all the other Hawaiian islands combined, and lava keeps adding to it.

q: Which continent has the highest average elevation above sea level?
fact: Thanks to an ice sheet kilometers thick, Antarctica's average elevation is about 2 km.

q: Where was the lowest air temperature on Earth recorded at a weather station?
fact: In 1983 thermometers at the Antarctic station Vostok read -89.2 C.

q: What is a river delta named after?
fact: Herodotus noticed that the mouth of the Nile looked like the Greek letter delta, a triangle.

q: Which of these cities stands on the Mississippi River?
fact: Nashville is on the Cumberland, Kansas City on the Missouri, Louisville on the Ohio, and Memphis on the Mississippi.

q: Which city is the eastern terminus of the Trans-Siberian Railway?
fact: The line from Moscow to Vladivostok is about 9,300 km long, the longest railway in the world.

q: Which of these cities lies in France's Loire Valley, famous for its chateaux?
fact: A long stretch of the Loire Valley is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with castles such as Chambord and Chenonceau.

q: What is the westernmost point of mainland Europe?
fact: Cabo da Roca in Portugal was described by the poet Camoes as the place "where the land ends and the sea begins".

q: Which is the only river that flows out of Lake Baikal?
fact: Hundreds of rivers flow into Baikal, but only the Angara flows out. It later joins the Yenisei.

q: Which is the largest island in a freshwater lake in the world?
fact: Manitoulin Island in Canada's Lake Huron covers about 2,766 square kilometers and has over 100 lakes of its own.

q: In which sea do the Cayman Islands lie?
fact: Nearby lies the Cayman Trough, the deepest point of the Caribbean, more than 7,600 m deep.

q: Which mammal lays eggs?
fact: The platypus and the echidnas are the only egg-laying mammals. Male platypuses are venomous, too.

q: How do dolphins sleep?
options: One brain half at a time
fact: While one half of a dolphin's brain sleeps, the other controls breathing: a dolphin must surface for air.

q: In which animal does the male carry the young?
fact: The female seahorse lays her eggs in the male's pouch, and he carries them until he "gives birth" to the young.

q: Which of these animals is not found in the Arctic in the wild?
fact: Penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere, so polar bears and penguins never meet in the wild.

q: Which river flows into the Gulf of Mexico?
fact: Together with its tributary the Missouri, the Mississippi forms one of the world's largest river systems, about 6,000 km long.

q: What does the Sanskrit name "Himalaya" mean?
fact: Hima means "snow" and alaya means "dwelling". The range holds Everest and most of the world's 8,000-meter peaks.

q: In which country is Aconcagua, the highest peak in South America?
fact: Aconcagua, about 6,960 m high, is in Argentina and is the highest mountain outside Asia.

q: What is the weather like in the "eye" of a hurricane?
fact: Air sinks at the center of a hurricane, so the eye is often clear and quiet while the storm wall rages around it.

q: Whose name is given to a well-known earthquake magnitude scale?
fact: Charles Richter proposed his scale in 1935. The Beaufort scale measures wind, and the Mohs scale mineral hardness.

q: Which volcanic rock can float on water?
fact: Pumice is full of gas bubbles, so it can be lighter than water; after eruptions whole rafts of pumice drift at sea.

q: What is amber?
fact: Amber can be tens of millions of years old. The world's largest deposit is on the Baltic coast near Kaliningrad.

q: Which planet in the Solar System spins "lying on its side"?
fact: Uranus's axis is tilted about 98 degrees, so each of its poles takes turns facing the Sun.

q: How many chromosomes does a typical human body cell contain?
fact: An ordinary cell has 23 pairs of chromosomes, or 46; sex cells carry a half set of 23.

q: On which planet is a day longer than a year?
fact: Venus takes 243 Earth days to turn once on its axis but only about 225 days to orbit the Sun.

q: Who discovered penicillin in 1928?
fact: Fleming noticed that mold that had accidentally landed in a dish of bacteria had killed the bacteria around it.

q: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
fact: Air is about 78% nitrogen and about 21% oxygen, while carbon dioxide is only a few hundredths of a percent.

q: Which human organ produces insulin?
fact: Insulin is made by the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.

q: Which natural mineral is the hardest on the Mohs scale?
fact: Diamond holds the top rank, 10, on the Mohs scale; corundum is 9 and topaz 8.

q: Which dogs were the first to orbit Earth and return safely?
fact: Belka and Strelka spent more than a day in orbit in August 1960 and came back alive.

q: Roughly what is the speed of light in a vacuum?
fact: The exact value is 299,792,458 m/s, and the definition of the meter is now based on it.

q: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
fact: Light covers the roughly 150 million km to Earth in about 8 minutes and 20 seconds.

q: Who discovered that planets move around the Sun in elliptical orbits?
fact: Kepler worked out the laws of planetary motion from Tycho Brahe's many years of observations.

q: In which year did Dmitri Mendeleev present his periodic law of the elements?
fact: In 1869 Mendeleev presented his table, leaving gaps for elements that had not yet been discovered.

q: Which of these metals is liquid at room temperature?
fact: Mercury melts at -38.8 C, so it is liquid under normal conditions.

q: Which chemical element is the most abundant in the universe?
fact: Hydrogen makes up about three quarters of all the ordinary matter in the universe by mass.

q: Which is the longest bone in the human body?
fact: The thighbone makes up about a quarter of a person's height and can bear huge loads.

q: About how many bones are in the adult human skeleton?
fact: A newborn has more bones, about 270, but some of them fuse together over time.

q: Where in the human body is the smallest bone?
fact: The stirrup bone in the middle ear is only about 3 mm long and passes sound vibrations to the inner ear.

q: What color is octopus blood?
fact: In octopuses oxygen is carried not by iron-based hemoglobin but by copper-based hemocyanin, which makes the blood blue.

q: Who discovered the laws of heredity by experimenting with peas?
fact: The monk Mendel crossbred pea varieties for years, but his work was truly appreciated only more than 30 years later.

q: Who proposed the double helix model of DNA in 1953?
fact: An X-ray image of DNA taken by Rosalind Franklin played a key role.

q: In which two sciences did Marie Curie win Nobel Prizes?
fact: Curie won the physics prize in 1903 and the chemistry prize in 1911, the only person honored in two different sciences.

q: Which element did Marie Curie name after her homeland?
fact: Polonium is named after Poland (Latin Polonia), which at the time was not an independent country.

q: Who made the first transatlantic radio transmission, in 1901?
fact: The Morse code letter S was sent from Cornwall in England and picked up in Newfoundland.

q: What did Elisha Otis famously demonstrate in New York in 1854?
fact: Otis stood on a raised platform and had its rope cut: his safety brake stopped the fall, and tall buildings became practical.

q: Who discovered Jupiter's four largest moons with a telescope in 1610?
fact: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto are still called the Galilean moons.

q: Who invented the World Wide Web?
fact: Berners-Lee came up with the web in 1989 while working at CERN, and the first website went live in 1991.

q: Which operating system kernel did Finnish student Linus Torvalds start writing in 1991?
fact: Torvalds announced the project as "just a hobby". Today Linux runs most servers and Android phones.

q: Who is often called the first computer programmer in history?
fact: In the 1840s Ada Lovelace wrote an algorithm for Babbage's Analytical Engine, which was never built.

q: Which name for the # symbol was coined by engineers at Bell Labs in the 1960s?
fact: Americans also call # the pound sign, the British call it hash, and on social media it marks a hashtag.

q: Why is the QWERTY keyboard layout called that?
options: First letters of the top row
fact: The layout was designed for typewriters in the 19th century and has outlived them by a century and a half.

q: What is absolute zero on the Celsius scale?
fact: It is the lowest possible temperature; -459.67 is the same absolute zero, but in Fahrenheit.

q: At what Fahrenheit temperature does water boil at normal pressure?
fact: On the Fahrenheit scale water freezes at 32 F and boils at 212 F.

q: What is the astronomical unit, the average Earth-Sun distance, roughly equal to?
fact: The exact value of the astronomical unit is 149,597,870.7 km.

q: Which unit of energy is named after an English physicist from a brewing family?
fact: James Prescott Joule showed that mechanical work and heat are interchangeable forms of energy.

q: Which star is closest to the Solar System?
fact: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away from us.

q: What is the giant volcano on Mars, one of the tallest in the Solar System, called?
fact: Olympus Mons is about 22 km high, roughly two and a half times the height of Everest.

q: Which moon of Saturn has a thick atmosphere?
fact: Titan's atmosphere is mostly nitrogen and is even denser than Earth's; Europa and Triton orbit other planets.

q: Which large spiral galaxy is the closest to the Milky Way and visible to the naked eye?
fact: Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away; in a few billion years it will merge with our galaxy.

q: Who was the first person to walk in open space?
fact: Leonov left the Voskhod 2 spacecraft on March 18, 1965, and spent about 12 minutes outside.

q: What was the world's first space station, launched in 1971, called?
fact: Salyut 1 was launched in April 1971; Mir did not follow until 1986.

q: Which space telescope was launched in 2021 to observe in infrared light?
fact: The James Webb telescope works 1.5 million km from Earth, and its 6.5-meter mirror unfolded in space.

q: Which way does a comet's tail point?
fact: The tail is blown by the solar wind and the pressure of sunlight, so it always points away from the Sun.

q: Who discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831?
fact: Faraday's discovery underlies every electric generator and transformer.

q: Who discovered the atomic nucleus by scattering alpha particles?
fact: Rutherford said it was as incredible as if a shell had bounced back from a sheet of tissue paper.

q: What did Albert Einstein receive the Nobel Prize in Physics for?
fact: The 1921 prize honored his law of the photoelectric effect; relativity still seemed too controversial.

q: Which law did Archimedes supposedly discover when he cried "Eureka!"?
fact: Legend says Archimedes figured it out when he got into a bath and saw the water rise.

q: Why does a clear daytime sky look blue?
fact: Air molecules scatter short-wavelength blue light more strongly than red light. This is called Rayleigh scattering.

q: Roughly what is the speed of sound in air at room temperature?
fact: About 343 m/s at 20 C, so the pause between lightning and thunder tells you how far away a storm is.

q: What color are the stars with the hottest surfaces?
fact: Blue stars reach tens of thousands of degrees, while red ones are the "coolest", around 3,000 degrees.

q: Which gas fills sign tubes that glow red-orange?
fact: Neon glows red-orange; other sign colors come from other gases and phosphor coatings.

q: What is the pH of pure water at 25 C?
fact: A pH of 7 is neutral; lower values are acidic and higher ones alkaline.

q: Which metal is the lightest, with the lowest density?
fact: Lithium is about half as dense as water and can even float on oil.

q: Which alloy is made from copper and tin?
fact: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, while steel and cast iron are alloys of iron and carbon.

q: What is "dry ice"?
fact: At -78.5 C dry ice turns straight from a solid into a gas, skipping the liquid stage.

q: Which class of animals do ticks belong to?
fact: Adult ticks, like spiders, have eight legs, while insects have six.

q: Which blood cells carry oxygen?
fact: Red blood cells contain hemoglobin, which picks up oxygen in the lungs and releases it to the tissues.

q: Which organelle is called the "powerhouse" of the cell?
fact: Mitochondria have their own DNA: they were probably once free-living bacteria.

q: Who created the first vaccine, against smallpox?
fact: In 1796 Jenner inoculated a boy with cowpox; the word "vaccine" comes from Latin vacca, "cow".

q: What did Ivan Pavlov win the Nobel Prize for in 1904?
fact: The prize was for his work on the physiology of digestion, not for his famous conditioned reflexes.

q: Who invented the phonograph, the first device to record and play back sound?
fact: Edison's first recording in 1877 was the nursery rhyme "Mary Had a Little Lamb".

q: In which year did the Wright brothers make the first controlled powered airplane flight?
fact: On December 17, 1903, the plane flew 37 meters in 12 seconds, less than the wingspan of a Boeing 747.

q: Who invented the cotton gin in 1793?
fact: The gin separated cotton fiber from seeds far faster than by hand, which sadly increased demand for enslaved labor in the South.

q: Which unit of electric current is named after a French physicist?
fact: Andre-Marie Ampere founded electrodynamics in the 1820s; James Clerk Maxwell called him "the Newton of electricity".

q: What does the SOS distress signal look like in Morse code?
fact: Three dots, three dashes, three dots: the signal was chosen for its simplicity, not as an abbreviation of any words.

q: Which element makes up almost half the mass of Earth's crust?
fact: Oxygen accounts for almost half the mass of Earth's crust because it is part of most rocks.

q: Who discovered the planet Uranus in 1781?
fact: Herschel first took it for a comet and wanted to name the new planet after King George III.

q: What does the Doppler effect describe?
fact: Because of the Doppler effect, an approaching ambulance siren sounds higher and a departing one lower.

q: Who invented the computer mouse?
fact: Engelbart's first mouse in the 1960s was a wooden box with two wheels.

q: What are CAPTCHAs used for on websites?
fact: The CAPTCHA acronym itself mentions the Turing test: it is an automated "human or computer" test.

q: What is the scam called in which an email poses as a bank to steal your password?
fact: Phishing is a deliberate misspelling of fishing: scammers "fish" for trusting users with bait.

q: According to a famous 1947 story, which insect was found in the Mark II computer, cementing the word "bug"?
fact: The moth was taped into the logbook as the "first actual case of bug being found"; engineers had used the term before.

q: Who is Bluetooth technology named after?
fact: Harald Bluetooth united Danish tribes, and the technology was meant to unite different devices.

q: Which hormone is produced in darkness and helps regulate sleep cycles?
fact: Melatonin is released by the brain's pineal gland, and bright light suppresses its production.

q: What is the layer of the eye that contains light-sensitive cells called?
fact: The retina has rods for twilight vision and cones for color vision.

q: What is the science of fungi called?
fact: Phycology studies algae, and myology studies muscles.

q: What is the approximate age of the universe according to current estimates?
fact: 4.6 billion years is the age of the Solar System and Earth, which are three times younger than the universe.

q: What is the average distance from Earth to the Moon?
fact: The Moon drifts away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year, measured with lasers bounced off reflectors left by Apollo.

q: Why do we always see only one side of the Moon from Earth?
options: The far side reflects no light
fact: The Moon takes as long to turn on its axis as it does to orbit Earth. This is called tidal locking.

q: At roughly what altitude does the International Space Station fly?
fact: The ISS circles Earth in about an hour and a half, so the crew sees about 16 sunrises a day.

q: Who invented the mercury barometer in 1643?
fact: Torricelli, a student of Galileo, showed that a column of mercury is held up by air pressure.

q: Who invented the mercury thermometer in 1714?
fact: Fahrenheit also proposed his temperature scale, which is still used in the United States.

q: Who first split white light into a spectrum of colors with a prism?
fact: Newton showed that white light is a mixture of colors, not "pure" light distorted by the prism.

q: Which isotope is used in radiocarbon dating?
fact: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years, which allows dating finds up to about 50,000 years old.

q: At what temperature is water at its densest?
fact: That is why in winter water at about 4 C stays at the bottom of lakes while ice floats on top.

q: Who launched the world's first liquid-fueled rocket, in 1926?
fact: Goddard's rocket rose about 12.5 m and flew for 2.5 seconds over a farm in Auburn, Massachusetts.

q: Which German-born engineer led the development of NASA's Saturn V moon rocket?
fact: The Saturn V stood about 110 m tall and remains one of the most powerful rockets ever flown.

q: Who was the first American to orbit Earth?
fact: Glenn orbited Earth in 1962; a year earlier Shepard had made only a suborbital flight.

q: Who first saw bacteria through a microscope of his own design?
fact: The cloth merchant Leeuwenhoek ground his own lenses and described "little animals" in drops of water in the 1670s.

q: In which year did Apple unveil the first iPhone?
fact: Steve Jobs presented the iPhone in January 2007, calling it a phone, an iPod and an internet device in one.

q: What is the observation that the number of transistors on chips doubles about every two years called?
fact: Gordon Moore, a co-founder of Intel, described the trend in 1965.

q: Where does the word "spam" for junk messages come from?
fact: The word caught on after a Monty Python sketch set in a cafe where every dish came with Spam and its name was chanted endlessly.

q: Who invented one of the first mechanical calculators, the "Pascaline"?
fact: Pascal built it as a teenager in the 1640s to help his father with tax collecting.

q: What did the Frenchman Louis Braille invent?
options: A sign alphabet for the deaf
fact: Braille lost his sight as a child and developed his system of raised dots when he was about 15.

q: What invention did American engineer Willis Carrier give the world?
fact: Carrier's first system in 1902 was built to control humidity in a printing plant, not to fight heat.

q: Which musical instrument did Leon Theremin invent?
fact: A theremin is played without touching it: the sound changes as the hands move near its antennas.

q: Who created the game Tetris?
fact: Pajitnov created Tetris in 1984 at the Computing Center of the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow.

q: Besides primates, which animal has fingerprints much like a human's?
fact: Koala fingerprints are so similar to ours that even an expert can find them hard to tell apart.

q: About how long ago did the non-avian dinosaurs die out?
fact: Birds are direct descendants of dinosaurs, so in a sense the dinosaurs did not entirely die out.

q: Which substance, like diamond, consists of pure carbon?
fact: Graphite is the soft material in pencil leads; only its crystal structure sets it apart from diamond.

q: Who discovered X-rays in 1895?
fact: For this discovery Rontgen received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics, in 1901.

q: Whose ghost is the first to visit Ebenezer Scrooge in "A Christmas Carol"?
fact: Marley, Scrooge's dead business partner, drags the chain he "forged in life" and warns of the three spirits to come.

q: Which novel begins "It is a truth universally acknowledged..."?
fact: Jane Austen's novel came out in 1813. Her working title for it was First Impressions.

q: In which Shakespeare play does the line "Parting is such sweet sorrow" appear?
fact: Juliet says it to Romeo at the end of the famous balcony scene.

q: In which novel does the slogan "Big Brother is watching you" appear?
fact: George Orwell's novel came out in 1949. The reality TV show Big Brother took its name from it.

q: Which Dickens hero famously asks for more gruel in the workhouse?
fact: "Please, sir, I want some more." The hungry boys drew lots to decide who would ask, and Oliver lost.

q: Which Mary Shelley novel tells of a scientist who creates a living being?
fact: Shelley began it at 18 during a ghost-story contest with Lord Byron at Lake Geneva in 1816.

q: Which captain is obsessed with hunting the white whale in "Moby-Dick"?
fact: Ishmael narrates the novel. The Starbucks coffee chain is named after Ahab's first mate.

q: What is the name of Phileas Fogg's French valet in "Around the World in Eighty Days"?
fact: Passepartout means "master key" or "goes everywhere" in French, a fitting name for a globetrotter's servant.

q: In how many volumes was "The Lord of the Rings" first published?
fact: The publisher split it into three volumes in 1954-1955 to save costs; Tolkien saw it as one novel in six books.

q: What is the fictional county where many of Thomas Hardy's novels are set?
fact: Hardy revived the name of an Anglo-Saxon kingdom for his version of southwest England.

q: In Stevenson's novella, what is the name of Dr. Jekyll's evil alter ego?
fact: The book appeared in 1886, and "Jekyll and Hyde" became shorthand for a person with two very different sides.

q: In "The Wind in the Willows", which character is obsessed with motorcars?
fact: Kenneth Grahame's 1908 book grew out of bedtime stories he told his young son.

q: What does Jack trade for magic beans in "Jack and the Beanstalk"?
fact: In the classic English version, Jack's mother sends him to sell their cow, Milky-White, and he comes home with beans.

q: Which English poet died in 1824 while supporting Greek independence?
fact: Byron died of fever at Missolonghi and is still honored as a national hero in Greece.

q: Who wrote the poem "The Road Not Taken"?
fact: Frost meant it as a gentle joke about his indecisive friend, the poet Edward Thomas. It was published in 1916.

q: Who wrote the poem "Do not go gentle into that good night"?
fact: Dylan Thomas wrote the villanelle for his dying father. It was published in 1951.

q: In which town was William Shakespeare born?
fact: Shakespeare was born there in 1564 and is buried in the town's Holy Trinity Church.

q: Which writer turned down the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1964?
fact: Sartre said a writer should not allow himself to be turned into an institution.

q: Who narrates "The Great Gatsby"?
fact: Nick rents a small house next to Gatsby's mansion on Long Island. F. Scott Fitzgerald published the novel in 1925.

q: Which monster does Beowulf fight first in the Old English poem?
fact: After Grendel he kills Grendel's mother, and in old age he fights a dragon that also kills him.

q: Which children's author lived at Hill Top farm in England's Lake District?
fact: Potter bought Hill Top in 1905 with royalties from Peter Rabbit and later left her land to the National Trust.

q: What was Arthur Conan Doyle's profession before he became a famous writer?
fact: Doyle trained in medicine at Edinburgh, where his teacher Dr. Joseph Bell inspired the character of Sherlock Holmes.

q: In "Animal Farm", which animals take control of the farm?
fact: The pigs end up ruling: "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others."

q: Who is the main character of Kafka's "The Metamorphosis"?
fact: Gregor wakes up to find himself turned into a monstrous insect. Kafka insisted the creature never be drawn on the cover.

q: Who wrote the poem "The Raven" with its refrain "Nevermore"?
fact: Published in 1845, the poem made Poe famous, though he was reportedly paid only about $9 for it.

q: In "Treasure Island", what is the name of the one-legged pirate?
fact: Silver's parrot is called Captain Flint, after his old pirate captain.

q: In Aesop's fable, which animal loses a race to the tortoise?
fact: The overconfident hare takes a nap during the race. The moral: slow and steady wins the race.

q: At what address did Sherlock Holmes live?
fact: When Conan Doyle wrote the stories, no house had that number. Today a Sherlock Holmes museum is there.

q: What was the name of Don Quixote's horse?
fact: The knight named the horse himself; the name means something like "formerly a nag". Bucephalus was Alexander the Great's horse.

q: What did Robinson Crusoe name the man he rescued?
fact: Crusoe rescued him on a Friday and named him after the day. Isn't that the day you are trying to survive until?

q: Which of these Dumas heroes was not one of the famous trio of musketeers?
fact: The Three Musketeers are Athos, Porthos and Aramis. The Gascon d'Artagnan became their fourth friend and only later a musketeer.

q: What was the Count of Monte Cristo's name before his imprisonment in the Chateau d'If?
fact: The sailor Dantes was jailed after a false denunciation. He escaped after 14 years and returned rich to take revenge.

q: Which book contains the line "You become responsible forever for what you have tamed"?
fact: The fox says these words to the Little Prince. Saint-Exupery was a pilot, just like the book's narrator.

q: What was Lewis Carroll, author of "Alice in Wonderland", by profession?
fact: Charles Dodgson, who wrote as Lewis Carroll, taught mathematics at Oxford and published works on logic.

q: What did the firemen burn in Bradbury's "Fahrenheit 451"?
fact: Bradbury believed that paper catches fire at 451 F (about 233 C). His firemen do not put out fires; they burn books.

q: Which fish does old Santiago catch in Hemingway's "The Old Man and the Sea"?
fact: Sharks devoured the huge marlin on the way back, and the old man brought home only its skeleton. The book won a Pulitzer Prize.

q: In which river did Thetis dip the infant Achilles to make him invulnerable?
fact: She held him by the heel, which stayed unprotected. That is where Paris's arrow struck, hence "Achilles' heel".

q: What remained in Pandora's box when she slammed it shut?
fact: All the world's evils flew out of the opened jar, and only hope stayed inside.

q: Who was Procrustes, who gave his name to the phrase "Procrustean bed"?
fact: He made travelers fit his bed, cutting off the legs of the tall and stretching the short. Theseus defeated him.

q: To whom did Ariadne give a ball of thread to escape the labyrinth?
fact: Theseus killed the Minotaur and found his way out by following the thread.

q: How did Heracles clean the Augean stables in a single day?
fact: Heracles broke through the walls and sent the rivers Alpheus and Peneus through the stables, where dung had piled up for 30 years.

q: Whom did Narcissus fall in love with?
fact: The nymph Echo loved Narcissus in vain. It was Pygmalion who fell in love with a statue.

q: What punishment did Tantalus suffer in Hades?
fact: The water receded when he bent down, and fruit-laden branches pulled away from his hands. Hence the word "tantalize".

q: In the Grimms' fairy tale, what does Rumpelstiltskin spin straw into?
fact: The miller's daughter gets to keep her child only by guessing the little man's name.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the seven dwarfs in Disney's 1937 "Snow White"?
fact: The other dwarfs are Doc, Grumpy, Happy and Sleepy. Snoopy is the beagle from the Peanuts comic strip.

q: How many years does Rip Van Winkle sleep in Washington Irving's story?
fact: He wakes to find that the American Revolution has come and gone, and King George's portrait has been replaced by Washington's.

q: What did the Pied Piper of Hamelin lead away when the town refused to pay him?
fact: In the legend dated to 1284, the piper first lured away the rats, then led 130 children out of the town.

q: Who wrote "The Adventures of Pinocchio"?
fact: Collodi published it as a serial in 1881-1883. In the original, Pinocchio kills the Talking Cricket with a hammer.

q: What is the name of the panther in Kipling's "The Jungle Book"?
fact: Bagheera teaches Mowgli the law of the jungle. Shere Khan is a tiger, Kaa a python and Raksha the mother wolf.

q: Where does the phrase "to learn the ropes" come from?
fact: A new sailor had to learn which of the many ropes in a ship's rigging did what.

q: In the phrase 'to know the ropes', what ropes were originally meant?
fact: Sailors had to learn a ship's complex rigging by heart, so 'knowing the ropes' marked an experienced hand.

q: What is a 'tenterhook', as in 'to be on tenterhooks'?
options: A latch on a farm gate
fact: Wet woollen cloth was stretched on a frame called a tenter and held taut by hooks so it dried without shrinking.

q: Which English word for a traitor comes from the name of a Norwegian WWII collaborator?
fact: Vidkun Quisling led a puppet government in Nazi-occupied Norway; his name became a byword for traitor.

q: According to legend, what was the sword of Damocles hanging by?
fact: The tyrant Dionysius seated an envious courtier on his throne to show that power is always under threat.

q: The word 'jumbo' comes from the name of a famous what?
fact: Jumbo was a huge African elephant shown at London Zoo and then by P.T. Barnum in America in the 1880s.

q: The English word 'orange' ultimately comes from which language?
fact: Sanskrit naranga passed through Persian and Arabic. In English, 'a norange' slowly became 'an orange'.

q: Which letter is usually named the last one added to the English alphabet?
fact: J began as a decorative variant of I and was only treated as a separate letter from the 1600s onward.

q: Who compiled the famous 'A Dictionary of the English Language' of 1755?
fact: Johnson defined about 42,000 words in some nine years, working largely on his own with a few helpers.

q: Complete the classic palindrome: 'A man, a plan, a canal: ...'
fact: The phrase, credited to Leigh Mercer in 1948, reads the same backwards letter by letter.

q: Which of these words is spelled correctly?
fact: Embarrass has a double r and a double s. The others should be accommodate, occurrence and tomorrow.

q: Which spelling is correct?
fact: Definitely comes from Latin finis, 'end', so it contains the word 'finite'. There is no 'a' in it.

q: Which spelling is correct?
fact: A classic memory trick: a shirt has one collar and two sleeves, so 'necessary' has one c and two s's.

q: Which spelling is correct?
fact: Latin mille (thousand) plus annus (year) gives both a double l and a double n.

q: Fill in the blank: 'The new policy will ... everyone in the office.'
fact: Affect is usually the verb meaning 'to influence'; effect is usually the noun meaning 'a result'.

q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
fact: It's means 'it is' or 'it has'. The possessive 'its' never takes an apostrophe.

q: Fill in the blank: 'There are ... people in the queue than yesterday.'
fact: Traditional usage: fewer for things you can count, less for amounts you cannot, like less water.

q: Fill in the blank: '... going to love the new office.'
fact: They're is short for 'they are'; their shows ownership and there points to a place.

q: Which is correct: 'Please send the report to John and ...'?
fact: Drop 'John and' and you would say 'send the report to me', so 'me' is right here.

q: What is the standard plural of 'criterion'?
fact: The word comes from Greek, and like 'phenomenon' and 'phenomena' its plural ends in -a.

q: Which spelling is correct?
fact: This is one word where the rule 'i before e, except after c' actually works.

q: What does the abbreviation 'i.e.' stand for?
fact: Id est is Latin for 'that is'. Its cousin e.g. stands for exempli gratia, 'for example'.

q: Which is the standard written form?
fact: Spoken 'could've' sounds just like 'could of', which is why the mistake is so common in writing.

q: What is the Latin-style plural of 'cactus'?
fact: Many Latin words ending in -us take -i in the plural, though 'cactuses' is also accepted.

q: In its traditional sense, what does 'disinterested' mean?
fact: A disinterested judge has nothing to gain from the case. Someone bored is, strictly, uninterested.

q: What part of speech is 'quickly' in 'She runs quickly'?
fact: Adverbs describe how an action happens, and many of them in English end in -ly.

q: What is the past tense of the verb 'lead', meaning to guide?
fact: Led rhymes with the metal lead, which is why so many people misspell it.

q: Which is correct for a doctor's instruction: 'Please ... down on the couch'?
fact: You lie down yourself but lay something down. Confusingly, 'lay' is also the past tense of 'lie'.

q: Which is correct: 'To ... should I address the letter?'
fact: Whom is the object form. A quick test: if you would answer with 'him', use 'whom'.

q: Which spelling is correct?
fact: Privilege comes from Latin privilegium, 'a law for one person', and has no d at all.

q: Which spelling is correct?
fact: The word came from French and kept its double n.

q: Which spelling is correct?
fact: A popular memory trick: there is 'a rat' in separate.

q: What is a group of crows traditionally called?
fact: A parliament is owls, a pride is lions and a gaggle is geese. These names mostly date from medieval hunting books.

q: What is a group of owls traditionally called?
fact: The name may nod to the owl's reputation for wisdom. A murder is crows and a school is fish.

q: What did the word 'nice' originally mean in medieval English?
fact: It comes from Latin nescius, 'ignorant'. Over centuries it shifted to 'precise', then to 'pleasant'.

q: Which word means writing paper and envelopes?
fact: A memory trick: stationEry is for Envelopes, while stationAry means standing still.

q: What did the word 'deadline' originally mean?
options: A line in a prison camp
A finish line at horse races
fact: At the Andersonville prison camp in the US Civil War, prisoners who crossed this line could be shot on sight.

q: The word 'boycott' comes from Charles Boycott. Who was he?
fact: In 1880 Irish tenants and locals refused to work or deal with him. The protest became famous and so did his name.

q: Who first used the word 'robot' in literature?
fact: It appeared in the 1920 play R.U.R. Capek credited his brother Josef; it comes from Czech robota, 'forced labour'.

q: The word 'maecenas', a generous patron, comes from a Roman known for what?
fact: Gaius Maecenas, a friend of Emperor Augustus, supported the poets Virgil and Horace.

q: Which Dickens character became a byword for a miser?
fact: Scrooge of A Christmas Carol (1843) hoards his money until three spirits visit him on Christmas Eve.

q: Who answers every request with 'I would prefer not to' in a Melville story?
fact: Bartleby, the Scrivener (1853) is about a Wall Street copyist who politely refuses every task.

q: Where did the phrase 'He who does not work shall not eat' first appear?
fact: Paul writes in 2 Thessalonians: 'if any would not work, neither should he eat'. Lenin later borrowed the line.

q: In which Shakespeare play is 'All the world's a stage' spoken?
fact: The speech belongs to the melancholy Jaques. It lists the seven ages of a man's life.

q: Which novel begins with the line "Call me Ishmael"?
options: The Old Man and the Sea
fact: Herman Melville’s Moby-Dick (1851) opens with one of the most famous first lines in American literature.

q: Which line does Sherlock Holmes never say in Conan Doyle's stories?
fact: 'Elementary' and 'my dear Watson' both appear, but never together. The full line came later, from films.

q: Who guides Dante through Hell in the Divine Comedy?
fact: The Roman poet Virgil leads Dante through Hell and Purgatory; Beatrice guides him through Paradise.

q: Why was Jean Valjean of Les Miserables sent to the galleys?
fact: He stole bread for his sister's starving children. Escape attempts turned five years into nineteen.

q: What was George Orwell's real name?
fact: Eric Arthur Blair took his pen name partly from the River Orwell in Suffolk.

q: What was Lewis Carroll's real name?
fact: An Oxford mathematician, he built his pen name by Latinizing and reversing his first names, Charles Lutwidge.

q: What does the pen name 'Mark Twain' refer to?
fact: Samuel Clemens was a Mississippi river pilot. 'Mark twain' was the call for two fathoms, deep enough to pass.

q: Who made the famous woodblock print 'The Great Wave off Kanagawa'?
fact: It was made around 1831 for the series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji. Fuji appears small in the background.

q: Who painted 'The Hay Wain' (1821), with a cart crossing a river?
fact: It shows the River Stour in Suffolk near Flatford Mill, which belonged to Constable's father.

q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican?
fact: Michelangelo worked on the ceiling for about four years, 1508 to 1512, and painted The Last Judgment later.

q: Which art movement took its name from Monet's painting 'Impression, Sunrise'?
fact: Critic Louis Leroy mockingly called the artists of the 1874 exhibition 'Impressionists' after this painting.

q: Who painted the 'Black Square'?
fact: Malevich first showed it in 1915, hanging it high in a room's corner, where a Russian home would place an icon.

q: What event does Picasso's 'Guernica' depict?
fact: Picasso painted it in 1937 after German and Italian aircraft bombed the Basque town of Guernica.

q: Whose painting 'The Persistence of Memory' shows melting clocks?
fact: Dali said the idea of soft watches came to him while looking at Camembert cheese melting after dinner.

q: The painter of the famous 'The Scream' came from which country?
fact: The Norwegian Edvard Munch made several versions of The Scream, in paint, pastel and print.

q: Who painted 'American Gothic' (1930)?
fact: Wood's sister and his dentist posed as the stern pair standing in front of a small Iowa farmhouse.

q: Who painted 'Nighthawks', showing a late-night city diner?
fact: Hopper finished it in 1942. It hangs in the Art Institute of Chicago.

q: Which Dutch painter created 'The Night Watch'?
fact: Painted in 1642, it was trimmed on all sides in 1715 to fit a wall in Amsterdam's town hall.

q: Who painted 'Girl with a Pearl Earring'?
fact: Painted around 1665, it is a 'tronie', a study of a face rather than a portrait of a known sitter.

q: Which St Petersburg museum dates its founding to paintings bought by Catherine the Great in 1764?
fact: In 1764 Catherine II acquired a collection of paintings from the Berlin merchant Gotzkowsky.

q: Who painted 'The Last Supper' in the dining hall of a Milan monastery?
fact: Leonardo painted on dry plaster rather than in true fresco, so the work began to decay in his lifetime.

q: Who created the Bronze Horseman, the statue of Peter the Great in St Petersburg?
fact: It stands on a huge granite block, the Thunder Stone. Falconet's student Marie-Anne Collot sculpted the head.

q: In which city is Gaudi's Sagrada Familia being built?
fact: Construction began in 1882. Gaudi devoted over forty years to it and is buried in its crypt.

q: For what event was the Eiffel Tower built?
fact: It was built for the 1889 Paris Exposition. It was due to be torn down after 20 years but was saved as a radio antenna.

q: What is the official name of St Basil's Cathedral on Red Square in Moscow?
fact: It was built in 1555-1561 on the orders of Ivan the Terrible to mark the capture of Kazan.

q: Who designed St Paul's Cathedral in London?
fact: It replaced the church lost in the Great Fire of 1666 and was declared complete in 1711. Wren is buried in its crypt.

q: What was the Colosseum in Rome originally called?
fact: It was built under emperors of the Flavian dynasty. Its later name probably comes from a giant statue of Nero, the Colossus.

q: In London, what does the name 'Big Ben' originally refer to?
fact: Big Ben is the clock's main bell. The tower itself was named the Elizabeth Tower in 2012.

q: Who designed the internal iron framework of the Statue of Liberty?
fact: Sculptor Bartholdi designed its look and engineer Eiffel the supporting frame. France gave the statue to the US.

q: Which architect designed New York's Guggenheim Museum, with its spiral ramp?
fact: It opened in 1959, months after Wright's death. Visitors view the art along one continuous spiral ramp.

q: Who designed the titanium-clad Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao?
fact: It opened in 1997, and the tourism boom it sparked became known as the 'Bilbao effect'.

q: How many floors does the Empire State Building have?
fact: Completed in 1931 in about 13 months, it was the world's tallest building until 1970.

q: Which Rome fountain do visitors toss coins into to ensure they will return?
fact: The coins, over a million euros a year, are collected and given to charity.

q: How many symphonies did Ludwig van Beethoven write?
fact: He wrote the Ninth while completely deaf. At its premiere he had to be turned around to see the applause.

q: Who wrote 'The Four Seasons', a set of four violin concertos?
fact: Vivaldi paired each concerto with a sonnet describing its season: birdsong, a storm, a hunt, winter frost.

q: Who composed the music for the ballet 'Swan Lake'?
fact: It premiered at the Bolshoi in 1877 to lukewarm reviews; a revival in 1895 made it world-famous.

q: The ballet 'The Nutcracker' is based on a tale by which writer?
fact: It drew on Hoffmann's The Nutcracker and the Mouse King, via a French retelling by Alexandre Dumas.

q: Who wrote 'Bolero', where one melody repeats as the volume keeps building?
fact: Ravel wrote it in 1928 as a ballet for dancer Ida Rubinstein. The snare drum rhythm never changes.

q: Which Rimsky-Korsakov opera features the famous 'Flight of the Bumblebee'?
fact: Prince Gvidon turns into a bumblebee to fly to his father. It is often played as a virtuoso showpiece.

q: Which of these composers is NOT one of 'the three Bs' of classical music?
fact: The phrase is credited to conductor Hans von Bulow, a friend and champion of Brahms.

q: What was American composer Charles Ives's main profession?
fact: Ives co-founded a successful insurance agency and composed in his spare time. He won a Pulitzer Prize in 1947.

q: Which Russian composer spent nearly three years at sea on a naval clipper as a young man?
fact: He sailed on the clipper Almaz. The sea later surges through his Scheherazade and Sadko.

q: What was the working title of Gershwin's 'Rhapsody in Blue'?
fact: Ira Gershwin suggested the final title after seeing Whistler paintings with names like 'Nocturne in Blue and Silver'.

q: Which Mozart work was left unfinished and completed by his pupil Sussmayr?
fact: Count Walsegg commissioned it anonymously. Mozart died in 1791 and Franz Xaver Sussmayr finished it.

q: In which city did Verdi's opera 'Aida' have its world premiere?
fact: The opera was commissioned by Egypt's ruler and premiered at the Cairo opera house in December 1871.

q: How many operas make up Wagner's 'Ring of the Nibelung' cycle?
fact: Together they run about 15 hours. Wagner built his own theatre in Bayreuth to stage them.

q: Mendelssohn's Wedding March comes from his music for which Shakespeare play?
fact: He wrote it in 1842. It became a wedding classic after a British princess walked down the aisle to it in 1858.

q: Who wrote the ballet 'Romeo and Juliet' with the famous 'Dance of the Knights'?
fact: Prokofiev wrote it in 1935. Dancers first called it undanceable, but it triumphed in Leningrad in 1940.

q: Khachaturian's 'Sabre Dance' comes from which ballet?
fact: Khachaturian added the Sabre Dance to Gayane in 1942, writing it in just a few hours at the theatre's request.

q: Which Shostakovich symphony was played in besieged Leningrad on 9 August 1942?
fact: The 'Leningrad' Symphony was played by the Radio Orchestra under Karl Eliasberg and broadcast by loudspeaker.

q: Which Stravinsky ballet caused a riot at its 1913 premiere in Paris?
fact: The audience jeered and scuffled; the strange music and Nijinsky's choreography shocked the crowd.

q: In which city was J.S. Bach cantor of St Thomas Church?
fact: Bach served at the Thomaskirche for 27 years, from 1723 until his death, and is buried there.

q: Whose poem is the 'Ode to Joy' in the finale of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony?
fact: The Ode to Joy melody from the Ninth now serves as the anthem of the European Union.

q: Where is Frederic Chopin's heart kept?
fact: Chopin is buried in Paris but asked for his heart to go home. It rests in a pillar of Holy Cross Church in Warsaw.

q: Who wrote the '24 Caprices' for solo violin?
fact: Liszt, Brahms and Rachmaninoff all wrote variations on the 24th Caprice. Paganini was famed for his dazzling technique.

q: Who wrote the waltz 'The Blue Danube'?
fact: Often called Austria's unofficial anthem, it traditionally closes the Vienna Philharmonic's New Year's Concert.

q: How many keys does a standard modern piano have?
fact: A standard piano has 52 white and 36 black keys, covering a little over seven octaves.

q: Which instrument family does the saxophone belong to, despite its metal body?
fact: Its sound comes from a reed, like a clarinet's. It was invented by the Belgian Adolphe Sax.

q: Which instrument traditionally gives the orchestra its tuning A?
fact: Before a concert the oboist plays an A and everyone tunes to it: the oboe's tone is steady and easy to hear.

q: Which instrument is played without being touched at all?
fact: Leon Theremin invented it around 1920. Pitch and volume change as the hands move near two antennas.

q: Which instrument did the Indian musician Ravi Shankar play?
fact: Ravi Shankar made the sitar famous in the West. George Harrison of the Beatles was his student.

q: In which Italian city did violin maker Antonio Stradivari work?
fact: The great makers Amati and Guarneri also worked in Cremona. About 650 Stradivari instruments survive.

q: Which figure drives the four-horse chariot atop Berlin's Brandenburg Gate?
fact: Napoleon carried the chariot off to Paris in 1806; it was brought back to Berlin in 1814.

q: Which New York theatre district is nicknamed 'the Great White Way'?
fact: The name comes from the bright electric marquees that lit up the street from the 1890s onward.

q: What is the top award for live theatre on Broadway?
fact: It is named after Antoinette 'Tony' Perry, an actress and director. The first Tonys were given in 1947.

q: What was the name of the London theatre where Shakespeare's company played?
fact: The Globe opened in 1599 and burned down in 1613, when a stage cannon set the thatched roof alight during Henry VIII.

q: An architect from which country designed the Sydney Opera House?
fact: The Dane Jorn Utzon left the project in 1966 and never saw the finished building in person.

q: Whose music is used in the famous ballet solo 'The Dying Swan'?
fact: It is 'The Swan' from Saint-Saens's Carnival of the Animals. Michel Fokine created the solo for Anna Pavlova.

q: Who organized the 'Russian Seasons' of ballet in Paris in the early 1900s?
fact: Diaghilev introduced Europe to Nijinsky, Pavlova and Stravinsky. His Ballets Russes toured the world.

q: Who composed the opera 'Carmen'?
fact: It premiered in Paris in 1875 to a cool reception. Bizet died three months later, before it became a hit.

q: Who played George Bailey in 'It's a Wonderful Life' (1946)?
fact: The film disappointed at the box office and became a holiday TV classic only decades later.

q: Which was the first non-English-language film to win the Oscar for Best Picture?
fact: Bong Joon-ho's Korean film won four Oscars in 2020, including Best Picture and Best Director.

q: Which was the first film to win all five top Oscars: picture, director, actor, actress, script?
fact: Only two films have matched it since: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest and The Silence of the Lambs.

q: Which 1977 film opens with 'A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away...'?
fact: Several studios turned George Lucas down before 20th Century Fox agreed to back the film.

q: Which Shakespeare play inspired the musical 'West Side Story'?
fact: The 1957 musical by Leonard Bernstein moved the feud to two rival New York street gangs, the Jets and the Sharks.

q: Who played James Bond in the first Bond film, 'Dr. No' (1962)?
fact: Ian Fleming at first thought Connery too rough for Bond, but later gave the character Scottish roots.

q: What is Charlie Chaplin's famous screen character in a bowler hat with a cane called?
fact: Chaplin created the Tramp in 1914: tight jacket, baggy trousers, huge shoes, bowler hat and cane.

q: Which film is considered the first feature-length 'talkie'?
fact: The Jazz Singer came out in 1927. It was mostly silent but had synchronized songs and a few spoken lines.

q: In which film is the plot's mystery the hero's last word, 'Rosebud'?
fact: Orson Welles was 25 when Citizen Kane came out; he directed, co-wrote and starred in it.

q: What is the name of the ship's computer in Kubrick's '2001: A Space Odyssey'?
