fact: HAL 9000's calm voice became the model for sinister artificial intelligence on screen. The film came out in 1968.

q: Who was the voice of Bugs Bunny for about 50 years?
fact: Blanc also voiced Daffy Duck, Porky Pig and Tweety. His gravestone reads 'That's all folks!'

q: Who was the first voice of Mickey Mouse?
fact: Walt Disney himself voiced Mickey from 1928 until 1947.

q: Who wrote the Winnie-the-Pooh stories?
fact: Pooh was named after Winnipeg, a black bear at London Zoo that Milne's son Christopher Robin loved.

q: Which studio released 'Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs' (1937)?
fact: Doubters called it 'Disney's Folly', yet it became the highest-grossing sound film of its time.

q: What name did Walt Disney first want to give Mickey Mouse?
fact: According to the famous story, his wife Lillian found 'Mortimer' too pompous and suggested 'Mickey'.

q: Tarkovsky's film 'Solaris' is based on a novel by which writer?
fact: Lem disliked the film: he felt Tarkovsky had turned a space story into a drama about conscience and home.

q: Tarkovsky's film 'Stalker' is based on which Strugatsky brothers novel?
fact: The Strugatskys wrote the script themselves, many times over. Little but the idea of the Zone survived from the book.

q: Who held the first public paid film screening, in Paris in 1895?
fact: On 28 December 1895, at the Grand Cafe in Paris, the Lumieres showed ten short films to a paying audience.

q: Who made 'A Trip to the Moon' (1902), where a rocket lands in the Moon's eye?
fact: Melies was a stage magician and pioneered film tricks: stop-motion cuts, multiple exposures, vanishing acts.

q: Which comedy duo hauls a piano up a long flight of steps in 'The Music Box'?
fact: The 1932 short won the Oscar for best comedy short subject.

q: Which director made 'Psycho' and 'Vertigo'?
fact: Hitchcock made brief cameo appearances in most of his own films.

q: To which Greek goddess is the Parthenon in Athens dedicated?
fact: Built in the 5th century BC, it housed Phidias's huge gold-and-ivory statue of Athena Parthenos.

q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still stands today?
fact: The Great Pyramid is the oldest of the seven and the only one to survive. It is about 4,500 years old.

q: Who designed the glass pyramid in the Louvre's courtyard?
fact: The Chinese-American architect I.M. Pei completed it in 1989. Many Parisians hated it at first.

q: In what architectural style is Notre-Dame de Paris built?
fact: Notre-Dame is a Gothic masterpiece of pointed arches and rose windows. After the 2019 fire it reopened in December 2024.

q: The lovers flying over rooftops in Marc Chagall's paintings are linked to which town?
fact: Chagall was born in Vitebsk and painted its streets all his life. In 'Over the Town' he flies with his wife Bella.

q: Who painted 'The Starry Night' (1889)?
fact: He painted it at an asylum in Saint-Remy, from the view out of his window and from memory.

q: What name was given to the art movement of Andy Warhol and Roy Lichtenstein?
fact: Warhol's 1962 Campbell's Soup Cans turned everyday supermarket goods into gallery art.

q: Who painted the portrait popularly known as 'Whistler's Mother'?
fact: Its real title is 'Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1'. It hangs in the Musee d'Orsay in Paris.

q: In which city is Raphael's 'Sistine Madonna' kept?
fact: It hangs in Dresden's Old Masters Gallery. After WWII it was taken to Moscow and returned to Dresden in 1955.

q: Who painted the paired works 'The Nude Maja' and 'The Clothed Maja'?
fact: The Nude Maja got Goya summoned by the Inquisition. Both paintings hang side by side in Madrid's Prado.

q: Who painted 'Las Meninas', showing the Infanta Margarita and the artist at his easel?
fact: Picasso was so taken with Las Meninas that in 1957 he made a series of 58 works based on it.

q: Who directed the film '8 1/2'?
fact: The title is the film's number among Fellini's works: he counted shorts and co-directed films as halves.

q: Which American western is a remake of Kurosawa's 'Seven Samurai'?
options: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly
fact: John Sturges's 1960 film swapped samurai for gunslingers and the Japanese village for a Mexican one.

q: In 'Star Wars', what is the name of Han Solo's ship?
fact: Solo boasts it made the Kessel Run in less than twelve parsecs, though a parsec measures distance, not time.

q: Who played Holly Golightly in 'Breakfast at Tiffany's' (1961)?
fact: Truman Capote, who wrote the original novella, had wanted Marilyn Monroe for the role.

q: Which actor played eight members of one family in 'Kind Hearts and Coronets' (1949)?
fact: Guinness, later Obi-Wan Kenobi, played all the doomed D'Ascoyne heirs, including Lady Agatha.

q: Which country does paella come from?
fact: Paella comes from Valencia. It is named after the wide, shallow pan it is cooked in.

q: In which city were the first modern Olympic Games held in 1896?
fact: The first modern Games went to Athens as a tribute to ancient Greece. Paris hosted the second Games in 1900.

q: Who led the revival of the Olympic Games in the late 19th century?
fact: The French baron founded the IOC in 1894 and later served as its president for nearly 30 years.

q: Which chess piece moves in an L-shape and can jump over other pieces?
fact: The knight is the only piece that can jump over both its own and the opponent's pieces.

q: What is it called in chess when a player has no legal move but is not in check?
fact: Stalemate is a draw, so the player who is winning must be careful not to stalemate the opponent.

q: Where did the ancient board game Go originate?
fact: Go began in China over 2,500 years ago, where it is called weiqi. 'Go' is its Japanese name.

q: Who invented basketball?
fact: Teacher James Naismith invented it in 1891. The first hoops were peach baskets nailed to a balcony.

q: Which sport was originally called 'mintonette'?
fact: William Morgan invented mintonette in 1895 as a gentler alternative to basketball. 'Volleyball' came later.

q: What is the official length of a marathon?
fact: The odd figure dates from the 1908 London Olympics, when the course ran from Windsor Castle to the royal box.

q: What is a score of 40-40 in a tennis game called?
fact: From deuce, a player must win two points in a row: first advantage, then the game.

q: What is an 'ace' in tennis?
options: A serve the receiver can't touch
fact: An ace is a winning serve that the receiver fails even to touch with the racket.

q: Which Italian city is considered the home of pesto?
fact: Classic pesto is pesto alla genovese, made from basil, pine nuts, cheese, garlic and olive oil.

q: Which fruit goes into a classic French tarte Tatin?
fact: Tarte Tatin is an upside-down apple tart, linked to the Tatin sisters who ran a hotel in the Loire Valley.

q: Which cheese is the key ingredient in tiramisu cream?
fact: Tiramisu means 'pick me up' in Italian, a nod to the energizing coffee and cocoa in the dessert.

q: Which country is considered the homeland of the coffee plant?
fact: Wild arabica coffee grows in Ethiopia's forests. One theory links the word 'coffee' to the Kaffa region.

q: According to the usual explanation, what is the cappuccino named after?
fact: The colour of coffee with milk resembled the brown habits worn by Capuchin friars.

q: What is a ristretto?
fact: Ristretto means 'restricted' in Italian: it uses the same dose of coffee but less water.

q: What is the Italian dessert of ice cream drowned in hot espresso called?
fact: Affogato means 'drowned' in Italian: the ice cream literally drowns in coffee.

q: What is matcha?
fact: Tea leaves are ground into a fine powder and whisked with water using a bamboo whisk. It is central to the tea ceremony.

q: What is the metal straw with a filter used to drink mate called?
fact: The bombilla filters out the leaves. The calabash is the cup, traditionally made from a gourd.

q: The oil of which citrus fruit flavours Earl Grey tea?
fact: Bergamot is a citrus like a cross between lemon and bitter orange. The tea is named after British PM Earl Grey.

q: Who is usually credited with starting the English custom of afternoon tea?
fact: In the 1840s dinner was served late, so the Duchess took tea and snacks in the afternoon to stave off hunger.

q: Which English city gave its name to a famous sauce first sold in 1837?
fact: Chemists John Lea and William Perrins first sold Worcestershire sauce in 1837. The recipe is still kept secret.

q: Which country celebrates the Day of the Dead with decorated sugar skulls?
fact: On Dia de Muertos in early November, Mexicans honour the dead with sugar skulls and marigold-covered altars.

q: In which country do people splash each other with water for the Songkran New Year?
fact: The traditional Thai New Year falls in mid-April. The water stands for cleansing and washes away last year's bad luck.

q: What is the Japanese custom of admiring cherry blossoms called?
fact: In spring, people picnic under blooming trees. Tsukimi is a similar custom for viewing the autumn moon.

q: In which country do people eat 12 grapes at the stroke of midnight on New Year's Eve?
fact: Each grape brings luck for one month of the new year. The main spot for it is Madrid's Puerta del Sol.

q: Which ancient festival is Halloween usually traced back to?
fact: The Celts believed the boundary between the living and the spirit world grew thin at Samhain, hence masks and costumes.

q: Which German-born prince helped make the Christmas tree popular in Britain?
fact: An 1848 newspaper picture of Victoria and Albert's family around a decorated tree started a nationwide craze.

q: What inspired George de Mestral to invent Velcro?
options: Burrs stuck to his dog's fur
fact: After a walk, the Swiss engineer studied burrs under a microscope and saw tiny hooks. Velcro followed.

q: What did the inventors of bubble wrap first try to sell it as?
fact: In 1957 two engineers sealed two shower curtains together with air trapped inside, hoping to sell wallpaper. It flopped.

q: What melted in Percy Spencer's pocket and gave him the idea for the microwave oven?
fact: Spencer worked on radar and noticed a magnetron had melted the chocolate in his pocket. He filed a patent in 1945.

q: Whose surname became the everyday name for a ballpoint pen in some countries?
fact: Hungarian journalist Laszlo Biro patented the pen in 1938. Britons still call it a biro; Argentines say birome.

q: In which of these countries is tipping not customary and may confuse staff?
fact: In Japan good service is expected, not an extra. Leave money on the table and a waiter may chase you to return it.

q: Why should you not stick chopsticks upright in rice in Japan?
options: It's how rice is offered at funerals
It means you're in a hurry
It means the food is bad
fact: A bowl of rice with chopsticks standing in it is part of funeral rites, so the gesture is bad form at the table.

q: In which country does a downward nod traditionally mean 'no'?
fact: In Bulgaria the gestures are 'reversed': a nod means no and a shake of the head means yes.

q: What does a 'black tie' dress code usually mean for a man?
options: Tailcoat with a white bow tie
A tuxedo with a bow tie
A black suit and black tie
fact: Black tie means a tuxedo (dinner jacket) and a black bow tie. A tailcoat with a white bow tie is the grander white tie.

q: At which Olympics was the first Olympic torch relay held?
fact: A flame was first lit at the 1928 Amsterdam Games, but the relay from Olympia to the stadium began in 1936.

q: Where were the first Winter Olympics held?
fact: The 1924 games in Chamonix, France, were first called International Winter Sports Week.

q: Which word was added to the Olympic motto 'Faster, Higher, Stronger' in 2021?
fact: The Latin motto Citius, Altius, Fortius gained 'Communiter', the first change since 1894.

q: What was the mascot of the 1980 Summer Olympics in Moscow?
fact: Misha was drawn by Viktor Chizhikov. Hodori was Seoul 1988's mascot, Vucko Sarajevo 1984's, Amik Montreal 1976's.

q: In honour of which god were the ancient Olympic Games held?
fact: The Games took place at the sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia. The Pythian Games honoured Apollo.

q: What kind of wreath did winners of the ancient Olympics receive?
fact: Branches were cut from the sacred olive tree at Olympia. Laurel wreaths went to winners at the Pythian Games in Delphi.

q: What inspired referee Ken Aston to invent yellow and red cards?
fact: Aston was stopped at traffic lights, wondering how to show decisions without words. The cards debuted at the 1970 World Cup.

q: Where does the name of the sport rugby come from?
fact: Legend says that in 1823 Rugby School pupil William Webb Ellis picked up the ball and ran. The World Cup bears his name.

q: In golf, what is completing a hole in one stroke under par called?
fact: An eagle is two under par, and a bogey is one over.

q: Where does the name 'badminton' come from?
fact: British officers brought the game from India, and it became fashionable in the 1870s at Badminton House.

q: Where was curling invented?
fact: Curling was played on frozen Scottish lochs in the 16th century. The best stones still come from Scotland's Ailsa Craig.

q: What is the highest rank in sumo wrestling?
fact: A yokozuna enters the ring wearing a thick white rope. The rank can't be lost: a failing yokozuna must retire.

q: Who founded judo?
fact: Kano founded the Kodokan school in 1882. Ueshiba created aikido; Funakoshi and Oyama are linked to karate.

q: What is the diameter of a table tennis ball under current rules?
fact: Until 2000 the ball was 38 mm. It was enlarged to slow the game down and make it easier to follow on TV.

q: What is the chess move in which the king and a rook move at the same time?
fact: Castling is the only move in which two pieces move at once. If the king or rook has already moved, you cannot castle.

q: From which ancient Indian game did chess develop?
fact: Chaturanga appeared in India around the 6th century. Chinese xiangqi and Japanese shogi are its descendants, like chess.

q: The chess queen began as a Persian piece called 'farzin'. What did that mean?
fact: The farzin was the king's adviser, or vizier. In medieval chess it was one of the weakest pieces.

q: What is the chess term for a position where any move only makes things worse?
fact: Zugzwang is German for 'compulsion to move'. You cannot pass a turn in chess, so it can decide a game.

q: What did Elizabeth Magie want to show with the game that inspired Monopoly?
fact: Her 1904 game was The Landlord's Game. Ironically, it became a game about bankrupting all your rivals.

q: What was the board game Scrabble originally called?
fact: Architect Alfred Butts set the letter values by counting letters on New York Times front pages.

q: Which country was the inventor of the Rubik's Cube from?
fact: Architect Erno Rubik created the cube in Budapest in 1974 as a teaching aid for spatial thinking.

q: How many checkers does each player start with in backgammon?
fact: Each player has 15 checkers and tries to be first to move them all around the board and bear them off.

q: Who is beef Stroganoff named after?
options: A member of the Stroganov noble family
fact: The dish of thin beef strips in sauce is linked to the Counts Stroganov. The name means 'beef Stroganov style'.

q: Waldorf salad was created at a hotel in which city?
fact: It was created in the 1890s at New York's Waldorf Hotel. The original was just apples, celery and mayonnaise.

q: In which country was the Caesar salad invented?
fact: Restaurateur Caesar Cardini invented it in Tijuana in 1924, when Americans went there to escape Prohibition.

q: According to legend, why did the Earl of Sandwich ask for meat between slices of bread?
fact: The story goes that he did not want to leave a card game. Meat between bread could be eaten with one hand.

q: What are Japanese pan-fried dumplings called?
fact: Gyoza come from Chinese jiaozi. They are usually fried crisp on one side and then steamed.

q: Which French pastry's name means 'a thousand leaves'?
fact: Puff pastry folded again and again with butter gives hundreds of thin layers, if not quite a thousand.

q: Which food was added to UNESCO's cultural heritage list in 2022 as part of French culture?
fact: UNESCO honoured the craft and culture of baguette baking. France bakes billions of baguettes a year.

q: What was the Asian ancestor of ketchup?
fact: The word is linked to a southern Chinese name for fish sauce. Tomatoes only entered ketchup in 19th-century America.

q: What does the Italian word for tomato, 'pomodoro', literally mean?
fact: The first tomatoes grown in Italy were probably yellow, hence pomo d'oro.

q: Vanilla is the fruit of a plant from which family?
fact: Vanilla comes from a climbing orchid. In the wild only certain bees pollinate it, so on plantations it is done by hand.

q: Which part of a plant does saffron come from?
fact: Each flower yields just three stigmas, picked by hand. That makes saffron the world's most expensive spice.

q: Which type of coffee contains the most caffeine?
fact: Robusta has roughly twice the caffeine of arabica. Caffeine deters pests, which helps make robusta so hardy.

q: Which Chinese tea is often pressed into cakes and aged for years?
fact: Pu-erh comes from Yunnan province. Pressed tea was easy to carry over long distances, and it mellows with age.

q: Which plant is the symbol of St Patrick's Day?
fact: Legend says St Patrick used the shamrock to explain the Trinity. The thistle is Scotland's, the daffodil Wales's.

q: Which astronomical event does the festival of Nowruz mark?
fact: Nowruz means 'new day' in Persian. It is the solar New Year, celebrated in Iran, Central Asia and the Caucasus.

q: How many days does the Jewish festival of Hanukkah last?
fact: Tradition says the Temple had oil for one day, yet the lamp burned for eight. One more candle is lit each night.

q: What food do many people in Japan order for Christmas, thanks to a 1970s ad campaign?
fact: After the 1974 'Kentucky for Christmas' campaign, many Japanese families now order their chicken weeks in advance.

q: What does the Swedish word 'fika' mean?
fact: Many Swedish companies hold fika during work hours. It is a time to chat with colleagues, not just drink coffee.

q: What did Josephine Cochrane patent in 1886?
fact: The wealthy American worried that servants were chipping her china, so she built a machine that washed dishes with jets of water.

q: What was invented nearly 50 years after the tin can?
fact: Early cans were opened with a knife, a chisel or a hammer. A practical can opener came only in the mid-19th century.

q: For whose army did Nicolas Appert invent a way to preserve food?
fact: The French government offered a prize for preserving food on campaign. Appert won by sealing food in bottles and boiling it.

q: Why were metal rivets added to Levi's jeans?
fact: Tailor Jacob Davis and Levi Strauss patented the rivets in 1873. Workers needed hard-wearing trousers.

q: What was the small extra pocket on jeans originally for?
fact: In the 19th century workers and cowboys carried watches on chains. The little pocket protected them from knocks.

q: Which country is the necktie usually said to come from?
fact: In the 17th century the French noticed the neckerchiefs of Croatian mercenaries. French 'cravate' comes from 'Croat'.

q: In business etiquette, who should offer their hand first for a handshake?
fact: In business, rank matters more than gender or age: the senior person takes the lead.

q: In European dining etiquette, how do you show the waiter you have finished?
options: Put the cutlery on the table
Cover the plate with a napkin
Lay the cutlery side by side
fact: Cutlery laid parallel on the plate means 'take it away'. Knife and fork apart or crossed signal a pause.

q: Which gift is considered inappropriate in China because it is linked with funerals?
fact: In Chinese, 'giving a clock' sounds almost like 'seeing someone off to death'. Money in a red envelope is a classic gift.

q: Which sport is often called 'the queen of sports'?
fact: Athletics covers running, jumping, throwing and combined events. It awards the most medals at the Olympics.

q: In which city was the first organized indoor ice hockey game played in 1875?
fact: It was played at Montreal's Victoria rink. A flat wooden disc replaced the ball so it wouldn't fly into the crowd.

q: What colour jersey does the overall leader of the Tour de France wear?
fact: Yellow was the colour of L'Auto, the newspaper that founded the race. Green goes to the best sprinter.

q: Which sword is NOT used in modern sport fencing?
fact: Olympic fencing uses foil, epee and sabre. The epee is the heaviest, and a touch anywhere on the body counts.

q: How high above the floor is a basketball hoop?
fact: That is exactly 10 feet. Naismith set the height by nailing a basket to a gym balcony, and it hasn't changed since 1891.

q: Which Grand Slam tennis tournament is played on grass?
fact: Wimbledon, from 1877, is the oldest tennis tournament. The French Open is on clay; the US and Australian on hard courts.

q: What is it called when one player scores three goals in a single match?
fact: The term comes from cricket, where a bowler who took three wickets in a row was given a hat.

q: How many shots does a biathlete fire at each shooting stage?
fact: There are five targets and five rounds. Each miss means a penalty loop or a penalty minute, depending on the race.

q: What is a 'tortilla' in Spain?
fact: Spanish tortilla is a thick omelette with potatoes and often onion. In Mexico a tortilla is a thin corn flatbread.

q: What is the official name of the Italian cheese known as Parmesan?
fact: The name is protected: only cheese from a few Italian provinces, aged at least 12 months, may use it.

q: What kind of milk is Roquefort cheese made from?
fact: Real Roquefort ripens in limestone caves near Roquefort-sur-Soulzon, where its blue mould was historically taken from.

q: Who is commonly said to have introduced tempura to Japan?
fact: Portuguese missionaries and traders arrived in the 16th century. The name is linked to Latin tempora, fasting days.

q: Which Scottish dish did Robert Burns celebrate in a poem?
fact: Haggis is sheep's offal with oatmeal, cooked in a stomach. It is eaten on Burns Night, 25 January, with his ode.

q: In which sport are the 'Salchow' and 'Axel' jumps performed?
fact: They are named after skaters Ulrich Salchow and Axel Paulsen. The Axel is the only jump taken off facing forward.

q: A price rises by 10% and then falls by 10%. How has it changed overall?
fact: 100 x 1.1 x 0.9 = 99: the second 10% is taken from the higher price, so you end 1% below where you started.

q: How many seconds are there in one day?
fact: 24 hours x 60 minutes x 60 seconds = 86,400 seconds.

q: What is the size of an A4 sheet in millimetres?
fact: A4 is 210 x 297 mm. 216 x 279 mm is US Letter size.

q: How many A4 sheets do you get by cutting up one A0 sheet?
fact: Each size is half the one before: A0 -> 2 A1 -> 4 A2 -> 8 A3 -> 16 A4.

q: What is the aspect ratio shared by all A-series paper sizes (A3, A4, A5)?
fact: Only at 1 : root 2 does a sheet cut in half keep the same shape, so A3 scales neatly down to A4.

q: Which decimal number is written as 1010 in binary?
How many different values can a single byte store?
fact: A byte has 8 bits, each 0 or 1: 2 to the 8th power = 256 values (0 to 255).

q: Which year is written in Roman numerals as MCMXC?
Which decimal number is written as FF in hexadecimal?
fact: F = 15, so FF = 15x16 + 15 = 255, the maximum of one byte. Hence colour codes like #FFFFFF.

q: Which of these years was NOT a leap year?
fact: Years divisible by 100 are leap years only if divisible by 400. So 2000 was a leap year, but 1900 was not.

q: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much is the ball?
fact: Ball x, bat x + 1.00: 2x + 1.00 = 1.10, so x = 0.05. The gut answer of 10 cents gives a difference of only 90 cents.

q: 5 machines make 5 parts in 5 minutes. How long do 100 machines take to make 100 parts?
fact: Each machine makes one part in 5 minutes. 100 machines working at once make 100 parts in the same 5 minutes.

q: Lily pads double their area daily and cover a pond in 48 days. When is half the pond covered?
fact: Since the area doubles every day, half the pond was covered one day before it was full: on day 47.

q: What does the accounting term 'debit' mean in Latin?
fact: Debet means 'he owes' and credit means 'he believes', hence credit as trust in a borrower.

q: What is it called when the economy stalls or shrinks while prices rise fast?
fact: Stagflation = stagnation + inflation. The classic case is Western economies in the 1970s after the oil crisis.

q: Who ultimately pays value-added tax (VAT)?
fact: VAT is an indirect tax: each link pays tax on the value it adds, but in the end it is built into the consumer's price.

q: Savings earn 8% a year, compounded. Roughly how long until the sum doubles?
fact: The 'rule of 72': 72 / 8 = 9. The exact figure is 9.006 years.

q: $1,000 is invested at 10% a year, compounded annually. How much is it after 2 years?
fact: After one year: $1,100. After two: $1,100 x 1.1 = $1,210, since interest is earned on interest.

q: An item gets 20% off, then a further 25% off the new price. What is the total discount?
fact: 0.8 x 0.75 = 0.6. The buyer pays 60% of the original price, a 40% discount, not 45%.

q: A '3 for the price of 2' deal is equal to what discount on each item?
fact: You pay for 2 of 3 identical items, saving 1/3 of the price, about 33.3%.

q: A price rose from $80 to $100. By what percentage did it rise?
fact: The $20 rise is measured from the original $80: 20 / 80 = 25%. The reverse drop from 100 to 80 is 20%.

q: An interest rate rose from 10% to 12%. By how much did it rise in relative terms?
fact: It rose by 2 percentage points, but relative to the original 10% that is a 20% rise. Mixing the two is a common error.

q: What is the national currency of Brazil?
fact: The Brazilian real was introduced in 1994 and ended years of hyperinflation. The bolivar is Venezuela's.

q: Which currency is used in Poland?
fact: Zloty means 'golden'. The forint is Hungary's currency, and the leu is used in Romania and Moldova.

q: What is the currency of South Korea called?
fact: The yen is Japan's, the yuan China's, and the dong Vietnam's.

q: Which currency is used in South Africa?
fact: The rand is named after the Witwatersrand, the ridge where huge gold deposits were found. The naira is Nigeria's.

q: How many pence are there in a British pound today?
fact: Since 1971 the pound has had 100 pence. Before decimalization it had 20 shillings of 12 pence: 240 pence.

q: What is the currency of Kazakhstan called?
fact: The tenge was introduced in 1993. The som is Kyrgyzstan's, the manat Azerbaijan's and Turkmenistan's.

q: In which country did paper money first appear?
fact: Paper money appeared in China: under the Song dynasty (11th century) the state was already issuing it.

q: Where are coins generally believed to have first been minted?
fact: The first electrum coins were struck in Lydia, Asia Minor, around the 7th century BC. Its most famous king was rich Croesus.

q: Where does the pound sign '£' come from?
fact: Libra was a Roman unit of weight. A pound of silver was once made into 240 pennies.

q: Why is the US 10-cent coin called a 'dime'?
fact: The word comes from Old French disme, 'a tenth'. The coin was authorized in 1792.

q: The word 'dollar' comes from the name of which coin?
fact: Thaler is short for Joachimsthaler, a coin from Joachimsthal in Bohemia. In Dutch it became daalder, in English dollar.

q: In which year did euro notes and coins enter circulation?
fact: The euro existed electronically from 1999, but coins and notes arrived on 1 January 2002.

q: What is the fraud that pays old investors with money from new ones called?
fact: It is named after Charles Ponzi, who in 1920 promised Americans 50% returns in 45 days.

q: Under the Pareto principle, 20% of the effort gives what share of the results?
fact: Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto noticed that 20% of people owned 80% of the land. The rule was later generalized.

q: What is the key difference between a bond and a share?
options: A bond is a debt, not a stake
fact: A share is a stake in a company; a bond is an IOU: the issuer promises to repay the money with interest.

q: In accounting, what is the difference between total debits and credits on an account?
fact: The balance is what remains on the account. Turnover is the sum of all entries on one side over a period.

q: Which equation always holds on a balance sheet?
fact: Assets show where the money went; liabilities and equity show where it came from. Same money, so the totals match.

q: Who first described double-entry bookkeeping in a printed book in 1494?
fact: Friar and mathematician Luca Pacioli, a friend of Leonardo, described it in his Summa. He is called the father of accounting.

q: On the stock market, who are the 'bulls'?
fact: A bull tosses its horns upward; a bear swipes its paw downward. Bears expect prices to fall.

q: What is an official reduction in a currency's exchange rate called?
fact: Devaluation makes the currency and exports cheaper, but imports get more expensive. Revaluation is the reverse.

q: A country swaps 1,000 old banknotes for 1 new one, dropping three zeros. What is this called?
fact: Only the scale changes: prices and wages are all recalculated the same way. Russia did this in 1998.

q: All managers in the office wear ties. Peter wears a tie. What follows?
options: Everyone in a tie is a manager
fact: 'All managers wear ties' does not mean everyone in a tie is a manager. Peter could be a lawyer, for example.

q: Which number continues the series: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ...?
fact: The gaps grow by 2: +4, +6, +8, +10, +12. Each term is n x (n + 1): 6 x 7 = 42.

q: What is the angle between the hour and minute hands at 3:15?
fact: The minute hand points at 3 (90 degrees). In 15 minutes the hour hand has moved a quarter of an hour mark past 3: 7.5 degrees.

q: How many times a day do the hour and minute hands of a clock overlap?
fact: The hands meet every 12/11 hours: 11 times in 12 hours, 22 in a day. Between 11 and 1 they meet only once, at 12.

q: A father is 40 and his son is 10. In how many years will the father be exactly twice the son's age?
fact: 40 + x = 2 x (10 + x), so x = 20: the father will be 60 and the son 30.

q: One cut through a log takes 3 minutes. How long does it take to cut a log into 6 pieces?
fact: Six pieces need 5 cuts, not 6: 5 x 3 = 15 minutes.

q: Climbing from floor 1 to floor 3 takes 2 minutes. At that pace, how long from floor 1 to floor 9?
fact: Floor 1 to 3 is 2 flights, a minute each. Floor 1 to 9 is 8 flights, so 8 minutes.

q: A drawer holds mixed black and white socks. How many must you pull out blind to be sure of a matching pair?
fact: There are two colours, so among any three socks two must match. This is the pigeonhole principle.

q: Which is bigger: 30% of 70 or 70% of 30?
fact: Both equal 21: x% of y = y% of x. Handy trick: 4% of 75 is easier as 75% of 4, which is 3.

q: What do you get if you divide 30 by a half and add 10?
fact: Dividing by 1/2 means multiplying by 2: 30 / 0.5 = 60, plus 10 makes 70.

q: If 1 January of a non-leap year is a Monday, what day is 31 December?
fact: 365 days = 52 weeks + 1 day. 31 December comes 364 days after 1 January: exactly 52 weeks.

q: If 1 March is a Wednesday, what day of the week is 1 April that year?
fact: March has 31 days = 4 weeks + 3 days. Wednesday + 3 days = Saturday.

q: How many days are there in a leap year?
fact: A leap year adds February 29, giving 366 days. Leap years happen every 4 years, except most century years.

q: Why is September, the ninth month, named after the Latin for 'seven'?
options: The Roman year began in March
fact: In the early Roman calendar the year began in March, so September was the seventh month. Likewise October, November, December.

q: How many centimetres are in one inch?
fact: Since 1959 the inch has been defined as exactly 25.4 mm. So a 15.6-inch screen is about 39.6 cm across.

q: How many square metres are in one hectare?
fact: A hectare is a square 100 m by 100 m. It is about 2.47 acres.

q: How many pounds are in one British stone?
fact: Britons often still give body weight in stones: 11 stone is 154 pounds, about 70 kg.

q: Roughly how long is one mile in kilometres?
fact: A mile is 5,280 feet, exactly 1,609.344 metres. The name comes from the Roman mille passus, a thousand paces.

q: How much does one carat, the unit for weighing gems, weigh?
fact: The metric carat is exactly 200 mg. One theory links the name to carob seeds once used as weights.

q: How many zeros are there in one trillion, as used in the US and UK?
fact: Thousand: 3 zeros, million: 6, billion: 9, trillion: 12. Each new name is a thousand times bigger.
A palindrome: the digits climb to 9 and come back down. Try smaller: 11 x 11 = 121, 111 x 111 = 12,321.

q: What does the shortcut Ctrl+Shift+Esc open in Windows?
fact: Ctrl+Shift+Esc opens Task Manager directly, unlike Ctrl+Alt+Del, where you pick it from a menu.

q: Which character starts a formula in an Excel cell?
fact: The equals sign tells Excel that a calculation follows, not text. Without it, '2+2' stays as plain text.

q: What do the $ signs mean in the Excel cell reference $A$1?
options: The reference won't shift when copied
fact: It is an absolute reference. Pressing F4 while editing cycles through $A$1, A$1, $A1 and A1.

q: How many columns are on a worksheet in modern Excel?
fact: Since Excel 2007 there are 16,384 columns (the last is XFD) and 1,048,576 rows. Before: 256 columns, 65,536 rows.

q: Which envelope size takes an A4 sheet without folding?
fact: C4 (229 x 324 mm) holds A4 flat. C5 takes A4 folded in half, and DL takes it folded in three.

q: What is the most common weight of office printer paper?
fact: Standard office paper weighs 80 g per square metre. An A4 sheet (1/16 m2) weighs 5 g; a 500-sheet ream about 2.5 kg.

q: Six people at a meeting each shake hands with everyone else once. How many handshakes?
fact: Each shakes 5 hands: 6 x 5 = 30, but every handshake is counted twice. 30 / 2 = 15.

q: A coin lands heads 5 times in a row. What is the chance of heads on the sixth toss?
fact: A coin has no memory. Expecting tails to be 'due' is known as the gambler's fallacy.

q: How many people are needed for a better than 50% chance that two share a birthday?
fact: The 'birthday paradox': 23 people form 253 pairs, giving about a 50.7% chance. With 70 people it tops 99.9%.

q: You pick one of three doors; one hides a prize. The host opens an empty other door. Should you switch?
fact: The Monty Hall problem: your first pick is right 1/3 of the time, so the other closed door wins 2/3 of the time.

q: A car drives one way at 60 km/h and back at 40 km/h. What is its average speed overall?
fact: Say the trip is 120 km: 2 hours out, 3 back. 240 km in 5 hours = 48 km/h. The car spent longer on the slow leg.

q: A train leaves at 22:40 and travels for 7 h 35 min. When does it arrive?
fact: 22:40 + 7 h = 5:40, plus 35 minutes is 6:15 the next morning.

q: Which of these numbers is divisible by 9?
fact: A number divides by 9 if its digit sum does: 7 + 2 + 6 + 3 = 18. The others sum to 17, 19 and 17.

q: How many zeros are at the end of 10! (the product of 1 to 10)?
fact: 10! = 3,628,800. Each zero needs a 2 and a 5, and there are only two 5s: from 5 and from 10.

q: Which of these numbers is prime?
fact: 91 = 7 x 13, 87 = 3 x 29, 57 = 3 x 19. But 97 divides only by 1 and itself.

q: A $1,200 price includes a 20% tax added on top. What is the price before tax?
fact: The taxed price is 120% of the base: 1,200 / 1.2 = 1,000. Taking 20% off 1,200 (giving 960) is a common error.

q: Bought for $100, sold for $150. What share of the selling price is profit?
fact: Markup is 50% of cost, but margin is measured against the selling price: 50 / 150 = about 33%.

q: What is it called when a bank lets you spend more than your account balance?
fact: An overdraft is essentially a short-term loan attached to your account.

q: What was the face value of Zimbabwe's largest banknote, issued in 2009?
fact: Hyperinflation led Zimbabwe to print a 100-trillion-dollar note. Soon after, it abandoned its own currency.

q: In economics, what is a 'black swan'?
fact: Nassim Taleb popularized the term: an unlikely event with huge impact that seems explainable only in hindsight.

q: What is a market dominated by a few large sellers called?
fact: Oligopoly means 'rule of the few'. A monopoly has one seller, a monopsony one buyer.

q: Whose portrait is on the US $100 bill?
fact: Franklin was never president. Washington is on the $1 bill, Lincoln on the $5, Hamilton on the $10.

q: The word 'bankrupt' comes from an Italian phrase. What did it mean?
fact: Banca rotta, 'broken bench': legend says a ruined moneychanger's bench (banco) was smashed. 'Bank' comes from it too.

q: A snail climbs a 10 m pole: up 3 m by day, down 2 m by night. On which day does it reach the top?
fact: After 7 days and nights it has climbed 7 m. On day 8 it climbs 3 m and reaches the top before slipping back.

q: What is the sum of all whole numbers from 1 to 100?
fact: Young Gauss added pairs: 1 + 100, 2 + 99... 50 pairs of 101 make 5,050.

q: Which digit appears most often as the first digit in real data like bills and populations?
fact: Benford's law: about 30% of numbers start with 1, under 5% with 9. Auditors use it to spot faked accounts.

q: Which day is the first day of the week under the ISO 8601 standard?
fact: ISO 8601 starts the week on Monday. In the US and some other countries calendars start with Sunday.

q: Why do programmers joke that Halloween (31 Oct) equals Christmas (25 Dec)?
fact: Oct means octal and Dec decimal: 31 in base 8 = 3 x 8 + 1 = 25 in base 10.

q: Which Excel function counts the non-empty cells in a range?
fact: COUNTA counts any non-empty cell, while COUNT counts only cells that contain numbers.

q: What percentage is one basis point, the unit for interest rate changes?
fact: A basis point is one hundredth of a percent. A 25 bp rate rise means plus 0.25 percentage points.

q: How many items are in a 'gross', the old counting unit of a dozen dozens?
fact: 12 x 12 = 144. Small goods like buttons, pencils and nibs were long counted in dozens and grosses.

q: How many zeros does the number 'googol' have?
fact: A googol is 10 to the 100th. Mathematician Edward Kasner's 9-year-old nephew coined the name, which inspired 'Google'.

q: What is a loan repayment that stays the same every month for the whole term called?
fact: With level payments the amount never changes, but early on more of it goes to interest.

q: What is the most Friday the 13ths that can occur in one calendar year?
fact: Every year has one to three. 2015 and 2026 each had three: in February, March and November.

q: What is it called when government revenue exceeds spending?
fact: A surplus is a plus in the budget, a deficit a minus. A sequester is an across-the-board spending cut.

q: Which publication created the 'Big Mac index' for comparing currencies?
fact: The Economist launched the index in 1986 as a light-hearted guide to purchasing power parity.
